glossary.name: Frame rate & pacing
glossary.intro: DF cares less about the average frame rate than how evenly frames arrive. A locked 30fps with perfect pacing often feels better than an unstable 45fps.
terms: Frame rate (fps)
Number of new images the game draws per second.
Whether a mode holds its target (30, 40, 60, 120) during heavy scenes.

A game is a fast slideshow. At 30fps each picture stays on screen for about 33 milliseconds, and at 60fps for about 17. Higher numbers look smoother and also feel more responsive, because the game shows the result of your button press sooner. Most console games target 30 or 60, and some offer 40 or 120 on newer TVs.
Frame time
How long one frame takes to make, in milliseconds. 60fps = 16.7ms, 30fps = 33.3ms, 40fps = 25ms, 120fps = 8.3ms.
The frame-time graph under their footage; spikes show hitches the fps number hides.

Frame rate is an average over a whole second, so it can hide problems. Frame time looks at each frame on its own. A game can average 60fps and still feel bad if a few frames take 50ms instead of 16.7ms. That is why DF shows a frame-time graph: a flat line means smooth, and spikes are the stutters you feel.
Frame pacing
How evenly frames are delivered. Good pacing means every frame is shown for the same length of time.
Bad pacing (16ms, 50ms, 16ms, 50ms) feels juddery even at a 30fps average.

A game locked to 30fps should show each frame for exactly 33ms. With bad pacing, it shows one frame for 16ms and the next for 50ms. The counter still reads 30, but motion looks jerky, especially when the camera pans. It is usually a bug in how the game hands frames to the screen, not a lack of power, so it can often be patched.
Locked / capped
Frame rate held at a fixed ceiling and never above it.
Whether the cap is solid or drops under load.

Developers cap the frame rate on purpose. A steady 30 usually feels better than a rate that swings between 35 and 50, because your eyes notice the changes more than the number. “Locked” is DF’s praise for a game that reaches its cap and never drops below it.
Unlocked
No cap; the game runs as fast as it can.
Usually paired with VRR. Without it, unlocked often means tearing or judder.

With no cap, the frame rate rises in quiet scenes and falls in busy ones. On a normal TV this looks uneven, with judder or tearing. On a VRR screen it can work well, because the display follows the game. Unlocked modes also show how much spare power a console has, which is why DF likes testing them on newer hardware.
Stutter / hitch
A single long frame causing a visible freeze or jolt.
How often and how long: one hitch a minute versus constant.

Most frames arrive on time, then one takes several times longer, and the picture freezes for a split second. The average frame rate barely changes, which is why stutter doesn’t show up in a simple fps number. The usual causes are loading new data, compiling shaders, or the processor being briefly overloaded.
Shader compilation stutter
Hitches when the game builds a shader the first time an effect appears, mostly on PC.
Whether the port pre-compiles shaders, often as a loading step at first boot.

A shader is a small program that tells the graphics chip how to draw a surface or effect. Consoles ship with these ready to go, because every console is identical. PCs differ, so the game has to build them on your machine. If it does that during play instead of on a loading screen, the game freezes briefly the first time each new effect appears.
Traversal stutter
Hitches while moving through the world as new areas stream in.
Common in Unreal Engine games; DF calls it out even on high-end PCs.

Open-world games can’t hold the whole map in memory, so they load the area ahead of you and unload what is behind. If that work lands on the same processor thread that runs the game, you get a hitch each time you cross an invisible boundary. It is common in Unreal Engine games and tends to repeat in the same places.
Judder
Uneven motion, often when the frame rate doesn't divide evenly into the display's refresh rate.
For example 45fps on a 60Hz screen without VRR.

A 60Hz screen refreshes 60 times a second. A 30fps game fits neatly: each frame is shown twice. A 40 or 50fps game doesn’t fit, so some frames are shown for longer than others and camera pans look uneven. The fix is a frame rate that divides evenly into the refresh rate, or a VRR screen.
1% lows / 0.1% lows
Frame rate of the slowest 1% (or 0.1%) of frames in a test.
A better measure of smoothness than the average.

Take every frame from a test, sort them from fastest to slowest, and look at the slowest 1%. If a game averages 60fps but its 1% lows are 30fps, you will feel regular dips. If the lows are close to the average, the game is consistent. DF uses these mostly for PC hardware comparisons.
Performance / Quality mode
Console options trading resolution and effects for frame rate, or the reverse. Quality is sometimes called Fidelity.
Which mode is worth using and how big the trade is.

A console has a fixed amount of power, so developers let you choose how to spend it. Performance mode lowers resolution and effects to reach 60fps. Quality mode keeps the visuals high and runs at 30. DF tests each one and usually recommends the mode that best holds its target.
40fps mode
A mode running at 40fps on a 120Hz screen. Its 25ms frame time sits halfway between 30 and 60fps in feel.
DF strongly favours offering it on consoles.

40fps sounds only slightly better than 30, but in frame time it sits exactly halfway between 30 and 60: 25ms against 33ms and 16.7ms. It needs a 120Hz TV, because 40 divides evenly into 120 (each frame is shown three times) but not into 60. It lets games keep most of quality mode’s visuals while feeling clearly smoother.
Balanced mode
A middle mode between performance and quality, often 40fps or a VRR target.
Whether it is a genuinely useful compromise.

Some games add a third option between performance and quality. It typically runs at 40fps on a 120Hz screen, or lets the frame rate float somewhere between 40 and 60 on a VRR screen. The idea is to keep most of the quality mode’s visuals with a smoother feel.
Frame generation
The GPU inserts AI-generated frames between real ones (DLSS Frame Gen, FSR Frame Gen, Multi Frame Gen).
Smoother motion but added input latency and artifacts. DF says it needs a decent base frame rate, around 60fps, first.

The game renders two real frames, then the graphics chip creates an extra one in between by estimating how things moved. The picture looks smoother, but the game doesn’t respond any faster, because the extra frames don’t react to your input. It works best when the real frame rate is already high. From a low base, it adds visible errors and laggy controls.
Base frame rate
The real, rendered frame rate before frame generation.
What actually sets how responsive the game feels.

With frame generation on, the number on screen is partly made of invented frames. The base frame rate is what the game really renders, and it decides how responsive the controls feel. 80fps from a base of 40 looks smooth but still responds like 40. DF always asks what the base is before judging a frame generation mode.
Simulation rate / tick rate
How often game logic, physics or animation updates. This can differ from the render rate.
Low-rate animation on distant characters looks choppy even at 60fps.

A game can draw 60 pictures a second while only updating its physics or animation 30 times a second. You then see things like cloth, enemies or the whole world moving less smoothly than the camera. Some older games tie game speed to frame rate, which is why they can’t simply be unlocked to 60.
Half-rate animation
Distant objects or effects animated at a lower frame rate to save performance.
A visible shortcut DF often points out.

To save processor time, the game updates faraway characters or effects every second frame instead of every frame. At a distance you rarely notice. It becomes visible when the cut-off is too close to the camera, and an enemy a few metres away moves choppily while your own character is smooth.

glossary.name: Resolution & upscaling
glossary.intro: Modern games rarely render at the resolution you see. DF counts pixels to find the real internal resolution, then judges how well it is rebuilt to 4K or 1440p.
terms: Native resolution
The game renders every pixel of the output, e.g. true 3840x2160 for 4K.
Rare on demanding console games now.

A 4K TV has about 8.3 million pixels. Rendering natively means the game calculates every one of them, every frame. It gives the cleanest result but costs the most graphics power, so few big console games do it now. Most render fewer pixels and upscale, and a good upscaler can look close to native for much less work.
Internal / base resolution
The resolution actually rendered before upscaling.
DF's pixel counts, e.g. 1080p internal upscaled to 4K.

This is the number DF cares most about. A game can send a 4K signal to your TV while only rendering 1080p inside and upscaling the rest. The internal figure tells you how much real detail the console is producing, and it explains why two “4K” games can look very different.
Output resolution
The final resolution sent to your display.
Often 4K even when internal resolution is far lower.

This is what the console sends down the HDMI cable, and what your TV reports. It is almost always 4K on PS5 and often 1080p or 4K on Switch 2. It says little about quality on its own, because the picture may have been rendered at a much lower resolution and enlarged to fit.
Pixel counting
Measuring stair-step edges in a still frame to work out internal resolution.
A core DF method.

DF finds a sharp diagonal edge in a screenshot and counts the stair steps along it. Comparing that count with the output resolution reveals how many pixels the game really rendered. Modern upscalers and anti-aliasing blur those steps, which is why DF sometimes says a game is hard to count or gives a range.
Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)
Resolution drops automatically in heavy scenes to protect frame rate.
The range, e.g. 864p to 1440p, and how often it bottoms out.

The game measures how long each frame takes. If frames start to run late, it lowers the resolution for the next ones, and raises it again when the scene gets easier. Done well, you barely notice. DF counts pixels to find the highest and lowest values, because a wide range (say 1080p up to 4K) means the image will look soft whenever the action heats up.
Aliasing / jaggies
Stair-stepped edges from too few pixels.
Shimmering edges, especially on fences, wires and foliage.

A screen is a grid of square pixels, so a diagonal or curved line has to be drawn as a staircase. With plenty of pixels the steps are too small to see. At low resolutions, or with no anti-aliasing, they become obvious, especially on thin things like wires, fences and railings.
Shimmering / specular aliasing
Flicker on thin or shiny details in motion.
How stable the image is when the camera moves.

Small or shiny details can be thinner than a single pixel. As the camera moves, they flick between visible and invisible from one frame to the next, so the image seems to sparkle or crawl. Foliage, chain-link fences, wet roads and metal edges are the usual offenders. Temporal anti-aliasing exists mainly to calm this down.
Anti-aliasing (AA)
Techniques that smooth jagged edges.
Which method is used and how clean the result is.

All anti-aliasing works by blending the colors along an edge so the staircase is less visible. The methods differ in where they get the extra information: more samples per pixel (MSAA), a filter over the finished image (FXAA, SMAA), or previous frames (TAA). Each one trades sharpness, stability and cost differently.
MSAA
Multi-sample AA: extra samples on geometry edges. Sharp but costly, rarely used now.
Mostly seen in older games or forward renderers.

MSAA takes several samples along the edges of each triangle and averages them. It keeps the image very sharp and was the standard in the PS3 and Xbox 360 era. Modern lighting methods make it very expensive, and it does nothing for shimmer inside surfaces, so most engines have dropped it for temporal methods.
FXAA / SMAA
Cheap post-process edge smoothing. FXAA blurs; SMAA is sharper.
Seen as low-quality fallbacks today.

These look at the finished picture, find high-contrast edges and smooth them. They cost almost nothing, which is why they were popular on older consoles and still appear on Switch. They only see one frame, so they can’t stop shimmer in motion, and FXAA in particular softens the whole image, including text and textures.
TAA (temporal AA)
Smooths edges using data from previous frames.
The modern default. It can look soft and leave ghosting.

TAA shifts the image by a tiny amount each frame and blends the results over time. That gives each pixel many more samples than one frame could, which removes both jaggies and shimmer. The cost is softness and occasional ghosting. Almost every modern game uses it, or an upscaler built on the same idea.
Temporal upscaling / reconstruction
Uses past frames and motion vectors to build a higher-resolution image from a lower one.
How close the result looks to native.

Each frame is rendered at a lower resolution, with the sample positions nudged slightly from one frame to the next. Over several frames the game has seen more detail than any single frame contains, and it blends them into one sharper image. It needs to know how every object moved. Where that information is wrong or missing, you see ghosting, fizzle or blur. DLSS, PSSR, TSR and newer versions of FSR all work this way.
TAAU / TSR
Upscalers built into engines. TSR is Unreal Engine 5's.
Common in UE5 console games.

These combine anti-aliasing and upscaling in one step: the engine renders below the output resolution and uses previous frames to rebuild the full image. They run on any hardware, which is why console games use them so often. Quality is usually a step below DLSS or PSSR, with more blur and breakup in motion.
Checkerboard rendering (CBR)
PS4 Pro-era method that renders half the pixels in a checker pattern and fills the gaps.
Artifacts on edges and transparencies.

Rendering every pixel of a 4K picture is expensive. Checkerboarding draws half of them each frame, in a pattern like a chess board, and alternates which half. It then uses the previous frame to fill the gaps. On still or slow scenes it looks close to full 4K. In fast motion the two halves don’t match and you can see sawtooth edges. Newer upscalers like PSSR and DLSS have mostly replaced it.
DLSS
Nvidia's AI upscaler on RTX GPUs and Switch 2. DLSS 4 uses a newer transformer model.
DF's usual benchmark for image quality.

DLSS uses a trained neural network to rebuild a high-resolution image from a low-resolution one plus previous frames. It usually beats non-AI upscalers at keeping fine detail stable. It is the main reason Switch 2 can show a clean picture from very low internal resolutions, sometimes as low as 540p or 360p.
FSR
AMD's upscaler. FSR 1 is spatial, FSR 2 and 3 are temporal, FSR 4 is ML-based on newer AMD GPUs.
Older FSR versions often show fizzle and disocclusion noise.

FSR works on almost any graphics chip, so it shows up on PS5, Xbox, Switch and PC. FSR 1 just enlarges and sharpens a single frame. FSR 2 and 3 use previous frames, which is much better but can fizzle and ghost at low resolutions. FSR 4 moves to machine learning, closer to DLSS and PSSR.
XeSS
Intel's upscaler; works across GPU brands.
Quality versus cost compared with DLSS and FSR.

XeSS is Intel’s answer to DLSS. It uses machine learning and runs best on Intel’s own Arc graphics cards, but a general version works on AMD and Nvidia cards too. DF usually ranks it between FSR and DLSS for image quality. It is a PC option and doesn’t appear on consoles.
PSSR
PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution, the AI upscaler on PS5 Pro.
How well each game uses it; results vary.

PSSR is Sony’s machine-learning upscaler, made for the PS5 Pro. It takes a lower-resolution image and rebuilds it to 4K, typically with sharper and more stable detail than the older FSR or TSR methods on the standard PS5. Early versions flickered in some games, especially on ray-traced lighting. An upgraded version, often called PSSR 2, arrived in March 2026 and DF found it gives a much better image in most games, with far less noise in Unreal Engine 5 titles.
QSSR
Sony's lighter AI upscaler for the standard PS5, based on PSSR.
Whether the sharper, more stable picture is worth the small frame rate cost on hardware without AI acceleration.

PSSR relies on extra AI hardware that only the PS5 Pro has. QSSR (Quick Spectral Super Resolution), announced in October 2026, is a streamlined version that runs on the standard PS5's ordinary graphics hardware. It costs a little more time per frame than older upscalers like FSR, roughly 1.5 to 1.8 milliseconds in DF's first test, so games may render slightly fewer pixels to make room for it. In return, fine detail like foliage and hair stays much steadier in motion. Games need a patch to use it. The first were Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei, followed in November 2026 by Marvel's Spider-Man 2, with Control Resonant, No Man's Sky, ARC Raiders, The Finals and Hell Let Loose: Vietnam announced. Sony says PSSR remains the best option on PS5 Pro.
MetalFX
Apple's upscaler on Mac and iPhone.
Seen in Mac and iOS ports.

MetalFX is Apple’s built-in upscaler for games on Mac, iPhone and iPad. It offers both a simple spatial mode and a temporal mode similar to DLSS and FSR 2. DF mentions it when testing big games on Apple hardware, such as the Resident Evil and Assassin’s Creed ports.
Spatial upscaling
Upscaling from a single frame only, with no history.
Softer and less detailed than temporal methods.

A spatial upscaler only has the current frame to work with, so it can’t invent detail that was never rendered. It enlarges the picture and sharpens edges. That is cheap and never ghosts, but results look soft or over-sharpened compared with temporal methods. FSR 1 and basic bilinear scaling are the common examples.
Upscaler presets
Quality, Balanced, Performance and Ultra Performance. Each lower preset uses a lower internal resolution.
DLSS Performance at 4K output renders 1080p internally.

On PC you choose how hard the upscaler has to work. At 4K output, Quality renders about 1440p, Balanced about 1250p, Performance 1080p, and Ultra Performance 720p. Lower presets run faster but give the upscaler less to work with. DF often describes console versions by the PC preset they match.
DLAA / native AA
Running the AI upscaler at native resolution purely for anti-aliasing.
Best image quality at the highest cost.

Here the upscaler isn’t upscaling at all. The game renders at full resolution and the AI model is used only to clean up edges and shimmer. It gives the best image quality available, better than standard TAA, but with none of the performance gain that upscaling normally brings.
Ghosting / trails
Faint copies behind moving objects left by temporal techniques.
Common around characters, birds and particles.

Temporal techniques reuse pixels from earlier frames. When the game misjudges how something moved, the old pixels are left behind and show up as a faint trail. It is easiest to see on small fast things against a plain background: birds, particles, a sword swing, or hair.
Disocclusion artifacts
Noise or blur where a hidden area becomes visible and there is no history for it.
For example behind a character's legs as they walk.

Temporal methods rely on what a pixel looked like in earlier frames. When a character moves and reveals the wall behind them, that wall has no history yet. For a few frames the game has to guess, so you see a smear or a noisy patch trailing the moving object’s edge.
Fizzle
Crawling, sparkly noise on fine detail like hair or foliage.
A common FSR 2 complaint.

Fizzle appears when an upscaler doesn’t have enough stable information about very fine detail. Individual pixels keep changing from frame to frame, so hair, grass, fences or distant trees look like they are boiling. It gets worse as the internal resolution drops, and it is one of FSR 2’s best-known weaknesses.
Motion vectors
Data telling the upscaler how each pixel moved between frames.
Missing vectors cause smearing on some objects.

For every pixel, the game records where that bit of the scene was in the previous frame. Temporal anti-aliasing, upscalers, motion blur and frame generation all depend on this. If something lacks correct motion vectors, often particles, water or animated textures, it will ghost or smear even when everything else looks clean.
Sharpening
A post filter that boosts edge contrast to fight softness.
Overdone sharpening causes halos and grain.

Upscaling and TAA soften the picture, so games add a sharpening filter to bring back some bite. A little helps. Too much creates bright halos around edges, called ringing, and makes noise more visible. DF often criticises over-sharpening, and praises games that let you adjust or turn it off.
Image quality (IQ)
Overall clarity, stability and sharpness of the picture.
DF's catch-all verdict term.

Image quality is DF’s shorthand for how clean the picture looks as a whole. It covers sharpness, how well edges are smoothed, and whether the image stays stable when things move. Resolution is only one part of it: a lower-resolution game with good anti-aliasing can have better image quality than a higher-resolution one without.
Supersampling / downsampling
Rendering above the display resolution, then shrinking it.
Cleanest image, very expensive.

If the console renders more pixels than the screen has and then shrinks the result, each screen pixel is an average of several rendered ones. That smooths edges and reduces shimmer very effectively. It is why a 4K game still looks better on a 1080p TV, and why older games look so clean on newer consoles.

glossary.name: Lighting & ray tracing
glossary.intro: Lighting is where DF spends most of its time today. The big split is between faked or precomputed lighting and lighting calculated live with ray tracing.
terms: Rasterization
The traditional way of drawing 3D scenes by projecting triangles onto the screen. Fast, but lighting must be approximated.
The baseline that RT is compared against.

Rasterization takes each triangle in the scene, works out which pixels it covers, and colors them in. It is extremely fast, and it is how nearly all games have been drawn for decades. The catch is that it doesn’t know how light travels between objects, so shadows, reflections and bounced light all have to be faked with separate tricks.
Ray tracing (RT)
Simulating light by tracing rays through the scene to find what they hit.
Accuracy versus performance cost.

Ray tracing follows the path of light. The game fires rays into the 3D scene and checks what they hit, which gives accurate shadows, reflections and bounced light without the usual tricks. It is very demanding, so console games normally use it for one or two effects and keep the rest rasterized.
Path tracing (PT)
Full ray tracing where light bounces many times and nearly all lighting is traced.
Most realistic and most expensive, e.g. Cyberpunk 2077's RT Overdrive.

Path tracing replaces almost all of a game’s lighting tricks with one system that follows light as it bounces around the scene many times. It is how film visual effects are rendered. In games it needs a powerful PC graphics card plus heavy denoising and upscaling. Cyberpunk 2077 and Alan Wake 2 on PC are the usual showcases.
Global illumination (GI)
Indirect light: light bouncing off surfaces to light other surfaces.
Whether rooms look naturally lit or flat.

In real life, light doesn’t stop when it hits something. Sunlight lands on a red carpet and tints the nearby wall red; a room is lit by light bouncing in from a window. Global illumination is the name for all that indirect light. It is what makes a scene look grounded instead of flat.
RTGI
Ray-traced global illumination.
A big upgrade; light reacts to changes live.

Here ray tracing is used for bounced light specifically. Because it is calculated live, the lighting responds when something changes: a door opens, a lamp breaks, the sun moves. That makes it ideal for open worlds with a day and night cycle, which is why games like Assassin’s Creed Shadows and Star Wars Outlaws rely on it.
Baked lighting / lightmaps
Lighting precomputed offline and stored in textures. Looks good but cannot change.
Breaks with time-of-day changes or destruction.

Developers run a slow, high-quality lighting calculation before the game ships and save the result as textures. At runtime it costs almost nothing, so baked games often run very smoothly. The limit is that nothing can change: no moving sun, and objects that move don’t affect the lighting. The Last of Us and many Nintendo games use it heavily.
Light probes
Points that store lighting so moving objects can be lit by baked lighting.
Low probe density causes light leaking.

Baked lighting is stored on walls and floors, so a character walking through the room would otherwise be lit wrongly. Light probes are invisible sample points scattered through the level that record the lighting at that spot. Moving objects pick up light from the nearest ones. With too few probes, characters can look like they don’t belong in the scene.
Light leaking
Light appearing where it shouldn't, like a glowing corner in a dark room.
A sign of approximate GI.

Cheaper lighting systems work at a coarse resolution, so they can’t always tell that a thin wall is in the way. Light from outside then bleeds into a sealed room, or a corner glows for no reason. It is a common weakness of probe-based lighting and of software Lumen, and ray tracing largely fixes it.
Lumen
Unreal Engine 5's dynamic GI and reflection system, with software and hardware RT modes.
Hardware Lumen looks better; software Lumen is cheaper.

Lumen gives Unreal Engine 5 games bounced light and reflections that update live, with no baking. Its software mode runs on any hardware using a simplified copy of the scene, which is cheaper but blurrier and prone to light leaks. Its hardware mode uses true ray tracing and looks more accurate. Console games mostly use the software mode.
Software RT vs hardware RT
Ray tracing on general GPU compute versus dedicated RT cores.
Hardware RT is more accurate and usually faster.

Hardware ray tracing uses special parts of the graphics chip to test rays against the real geometry, which is accurate but demanding. Software ray tracing traces against a simplified version of the scene using ordinary graphics power. It is cheaper and works on more hardware, but misses fine detail and can’t properly reflect characters or small objects.
Ambient occlusion (AO)
Darkening in creases and corners where light is blocked.
Without it, objects look like they float.

Where two surfaces meet, such as the base of a wall, under a car, or the folds of clothing, less ambient light gets in, so those spots are a little darker. Ambient occlusion adds that shading. Without it objects look like they are floating. With too much, everything gets a dirty outline.
SSAO / HBAO / GTAO
Screen-space AO methods of increasing quality.
Haloing around characters and missing shadowing off-screen.

These estimate ambient occlusion from the depth of what is on screen. SSAO is the oldest and roughest, often leaving dark halos around objects. HBAO is more accurate, and GTAO is the current standard on consoles, with more natural shading. All of them share the screen-space weakness: the effect disappears at the screen edges and behind objects.
RTAO
Ray-traced ambient occlusion.
More accurate contact darkening.

This uses rays to check how enclosed each point really is, so the contact shading is accurate and doesn’t depend on what is on screen. It removes the dark halos that screen-space methods leave around characters. It is one of the cheaper ray-tracing effects, so it sometimes appears in console quality modes.
Screen-space reflections (SSR)
Reflections built only from what's on screen.
Reflections vanish when the object leaves view or is blocked.

To make a reflection, the game looks at the picture it has already drawn and copies the right part onto the shiny surface. That is cheap and often looks great. But it only knows about what is on screen. Tilt the camera down at a puddle and the reflection of the sky disappears, because the sky is no longer in the picture.
RT reflections
Reflections calculated with ray tracing, including off-screen objects.
One of the clearest RT upgrades.

The game fires rays from the reflective surface into the 3D world to find out what should really be reflected. That includes things behind you or above the screen, and the reflection stays stable as the camera moves. It costs far more graphics power than screen-space reflections, so consoles often run it at reduced resolution or only on very shiny surfaces.
Cube maps
Pre-captured images used for cheap reflections.
Static and often mismatched with the scene.

A cube map is a 360-degree snapshot of the surroundings, taken in advance from one point. Shiny objects nearby show that image as their reflection. It is very cheap, but the reflection doesn’t include moving things like characters, and it looks wrong as you move away from where the snapshot was taken.
Shadow maps
Shadows made by rendering the scene from the light's point of view.
Low-res shadow maps look blocky or blurry.

The game draws the scene from the light’s position and records how far the light can see. Anything further away than that must be in shadow. It is fast and has been the standard method for twenty years. Because the map has a limited resolution, shadows can look blocky up close or flicker at their edges.
Cascaded shadow maps (CSM)
Several shadow maps at different distances, with more detail near the camera.
Visible cascade transitions as you move.

One shadow map can’t cover a whole landscape in detail. So the game uses several: a sharp one for the area near the camera and progressively coarser ones further out. You can sometimes see the boundary as a line moving ahead of you, where shadows suddenly become sharper.
Shadow draw distance
How far away shadows still render.
Shadows popping in as you approach.

Beyond a certain distance the game stops drawing shadows to save performance. Distant hills and buildings then look flat and oddly bright, and you may see shadows appear as you approach. It is one of the most common settings reduced in performance modes and on weaker consoles.
Contact shadows
Small, sharp shadows where objects touch surfaces.
Grounds objects in the scene.

Regular shadow maps are too coarse to capture tiny shadows, like the one under a cup or where a boot meets the ground. Contact shadows add them, usually with a short screen-space trace. They are a small effect that does a lot to make objects feel attached to the surfaces they rest on.
RT shadows
Ray-traced shadows with natural softening by distance.
Accuracy of soft shadow edges.

Real shadows are sharp near the object that casts them and get softer further away. Shadow maps struggle to do that; ray-traced shadows do it naturally. They also avoid the blockiness and flicker of shadow maps. The cost rises with the number of lights, so games often limit them to the sun.
Penumbra
The soft edge of a shadow.
Realistic shadows are sharp near the object and blur further away.

A light source has size, so the edge of a shadow is a gradient where the light is only partly blocked. That soft band is the penumbra. It is narrow close to the object and wide far from it. Getting this right is one of the clearest visual differences between ray-traced and traditional shadows.
Denoising / denoiser
Cleans up the noisy image produced by tracing few rays per pixel.
Boiling, smearing or lag in RT lighting.

Games can only afford to trace one or two rays per pixel, which gives a grainy, speckled result. A denoiser smooths that out by blending nearby pixels and previous frames. It makes real-time ray tracing possible, but it can blur fine detail and cause lighting to lag or smear when things change quickly.
Ray Reconstruction
Nvidia's AI denoiser built into DLSS.
Sharper, more responsive RT than standard denoisers.

Normally a game denoises its ray tracing and then upscales the result, as two separate steps. Ray Reconstruction replaces both with one AI model trained for the job. Reflections and lighting come out sharper and respond faster to changes. It is a PC feature on Nvidia RTX cards, used mainly in path-traced games.
Rays per pixel (rpp)
How many rays are traced for each pixel.
Fewer rays means more noise and more denoising.

More rays give a cleaner, more accurate result but cost more. Films use hundreds or thousands per pixel. Games typically use one or two, sometimes less than one by tracing at reduced resolution, and rely on a denoiser to fill in the rest. This is why ray-traced effects in games can look noisy or soft.
BVH
Bounding volume hierarchy: the data structure RT uses to find what rays hit.
Building it costs CPU time, a common RT bottleneck.

Checking a ray against every triangle in a scene would be far too slow. A BVH groups triangles into nested boxes, so a ray can skip whole regions it clearly misses. Building and updating this structure costs processor time and memory, which is why ray tracing can strain the CPU as well as the graphics chip.
ReSTIR
A sampling technique that lets games handle many lights with RT efficiently.
Behind modern path tracing.

A night-time city might have thousands of lights, far too many to trace rays to each one. ReSTIR picks the lights most likely to matter for each pixel and shares those choices with neighbouring pixels and previous frames. It is the key technique behind path tracing in Cyberpunk 2077 and similar games.
Emissive lighting
Glowing surfaces like screens and neon that actually light the scene.
Shows off RTGI and path tracing.

In older games a neon sign looked bright but didn’t light anything around it; artists had to place a separate invisible light nearby. With ray-traced or Lumen lighting, a glowing surface can cast real light onto its surroundings. This is a big part of why modern night scenes look so rich.
Volumetric lighting / fog
Light visible in the air, like god rays or misty beams.
Resolution and stability of the fog.

The game simulates light scattering through fog, dust or smoke, so you see beams through windows and haze around street lamps. It adds a lot of atmosphere. It is also expensive, so it is usually calculated at low resolution, which can make the beams look blocky or flicker.
Physically based rendering (PBR)
Materials defined by real-world properties like roughness and metalness.
Whether surfaces react to light believably.

Instead of artists painting how shiny something should look, they describe what it is made of: how rough, how metallic. The engine then works out how it reacts to light. The benefit is consistency. A material looks right in sunlight, at night or indoors without being adjusted for each scene.
Subsurface scattering (SSS)
Light passing into skin, wax or leaves and scattering inside.
Makes skin look soft rather than plastic.

Skin isn’t opaque. Light enters, bounces around underneath and comes out nearby, which gives the soft glow you see on ears and noses in bright light. Without this effect, characters look like plastic or stone. The same technique is used for candles, leaves, marble and snow.

glossary.name: Geometry & textures
glossary.intro: How much detail is in the world and how smoothly it loads in as you move.
terms: Polygons / triangles
The flat shapes 3D models are built from.
Polygon count sets how smooth and detailed models are.

Every object in a 3D game is a shell made of triangles. More triangles allow rounder curves and finer detail, like individual bricks or folds in cloth. Each one costs graphics power, so developers spend them where you will notice and save elsewhere. Modern characters use hundreds of thousands; PS1-era ones used a few hundred.
Level of detail (LOD)
Simpler versions of models swapped in at a distance.
How aggressive the swaps are on each platform.

Artists build each object several times, from a detailed version down to a very simple one. The engine picks one based on how far away it is, because a rock that covers ten pixels doesn’t need thousands of triangles. This saves a huge amount of work. The weakness is the switch between versions, which you can sometimes see happen.
Pop-in
Objects, shadows or detail suddenly appearing as you approach.
Distance and visibility of pop-in.

Games only draw detail near the camera. As you move, new objects, shadows and textures have to appear, and if that happens too close or too suddenly, you see them snap into view. It is most obvious when moving fast through open worlds. Slow storage, limited memory and short draw distances all make it worse.
LOD transitions
The moment a model swaps detail level.
Visible snaps versus smooth fades.

When an object switches from a simple model to a detailed one, the change can be an instant swap or a gradual blend. An instant swap is visible as a small jump in shape. A blend, often done with a dither pattern, hides it better. DF looks at how close to the camera these swaps happen.
Draw distance
How far away objects are rendered at all.
Often cut on weaker hardware like Series S or Switch.

Past a set distance the game stops drawing certain things entirely: grass, small rocks, people, cars. A short draw distance makes the world look bare in the distance and causes things to appear as you approach. It affects the processor as well as the graphics chip, so it is often reduced on weaker consoles.
Nanite
Unreal Engine 5's virtualized geometry, streaming film-quality detail with near-invisible LOD changes.
Near-zero pop-in, but heavy on performance.

Normally artists build several versions of every model and the engine swaps between them. Nanite does this automatically and continuously, drawing only as many triangles as the screen can show. Detail changes so gradually that pop-in nearly disappears. It has a fixed overhead, though, which is one reason Unreal Engine 5 games are demanding.
Mesh shaders
A modern GPU feature giving finer control over geometry processing.
Some new games require GPUs that support them.

Mesh shaders let the graphics chip handle geometry in small clusters and throw away the invisible ones very early. That makes extremely detailed scenes practical. They need recent hardware, so a game that requires them, such as Alan Wake 2, won’t run properly on older graphics cards.
Tessellation
The GPU subdividing surfaces into more triangles for extra detail.
Older technique, used on terrain and characters.

The game sends a simple shape and the graphics chip splits it into many smaller triangles, often pushing them in or out to form real bumps. It is used for terrain, cobblestones, snow and water. It was a headline feature around 2010 and is less talked about now that Nanite handles detail differently.
Culling
Skipping work on things the camera can't see (frustum or occlusion culling).
Failures make hidden objects cost performance.

A game world contains far more than you can see at any moment. Culling removes whatever is outside the camera’s view or hidden behind walls before any drawing happens. Good culling is a big part of performance. When it goes wrong, you may see objects vanish at the screen edge or appear late around corners.
Texture resolution
Detail level of the images wrapped on 3D models.
Blurry textures on low VRAM settings or weaker consoles.

Textures are the images that give surfaces their color and detail. Higher-resolution ones stay sharp when you get close; low ones turn blurry or blocky. They use a lot of memory but little processing power, so texture quality mostly depends on how much memory a console has. It is a common cut on Switch and Series S.
Texture filtering
How textures look at angles and at a distance.
Blurry ground textures at a glancing angle.

A texture viewed at a steep angle or from far away has to be squeezed into fewer pixels. Filtering decides how that is done. Poor filtering makes roads and floors turn blurry a short distance ahead of you. Good filtering keeps them crisp into the distance, and costs very little on modern hardware.
Anisotropic filtering (AF)
Filtering that keeps angled textures sharp, e.g. 16x AF.
DF often criticises low AF on consoles; 16x is cheap on PC.

This is the filter that keeps ground textures sharp when you look along them. It comes in levels from 2x to 16x. On PC, 16x is almost free. Consoles sometimes use only 4x or 8x because of memory speed limits, and DF notices because road markings and floor tiles smear into a blur.
Mipmaps
Smaller pre-made versions of a texture for distant use.
The wrong mip choice causes blur or shimmer.

A full-size texture on a tiny distant object would shimmer badly and waste memory. So each texture is stored with a chain of smaller copies, and the game picks the one that matches the object’s size on screen. When the wrong one is chosen, or it loads late, surfaces look blurry.
Texture streaming
Loading textures in and out of memory as needed.
Late-loading textures or low-res textures that never resolve.

A game’s textures don’t all fit in memory, so the engine keeps loading the ones near you and dropping the ones you left behind. When it can’t keep up, you see blurry surfaces that sharpen a moment later. Fast SSDs help a lot, which is why this was far more common on PS4 than PS5.
VRAM budget
How much graphics memory textures and data can use.
Running out causes stutter or blurry textures on 8GB GPUs.

Each game decides how much memory to give textures, geometry and other graphics data. If a scene needs more than the budget, the game has to use lower-quality textures or keep swapping data, which causes stutter. This is why PC cards with 8GB struggle in some recent games, and why Series S often gets lower-resolution textures.
Asset streaming
Loading world data from storage while you play.
Traversal stutter and loading pop-in.

Open worlds are too big to load all at once, so the game reads models, textures and sounds from storage as you move. If the drive or processor can’t keep up, you get pop-in or stutter. Consoles with fast SSDs made this far smoother, and it enabled things like Ratchet & Clank’s instant world switches.
Normal maps
Textures that fake surface bumps and dents through lighting.
Adds detail without extra polygons.

A normal map is a texture that tells the lighting which way each tiny part of a surface faces. A flat wall can then catch light as if it had bricks, cracks and rivets, with no extra triangles. Nearly every surface in modern games uses one. Viewed from a sharp angle, the illusion breaks and the surface looks flat.
Parallax occlusion mapping (POM)
Textures that fake depth, so bricks or stones look raised.
A cheap way to add depth to ground and walls.

This goes a step beyond normal maps. It shifts the texture depending on your viewing angle, so raised parts appear to hide the parts behind them. Cobblestones, rubble and brick walls look properly 3D even though the surface is still flat. The effect fails at the very edge of the object, where the outline stays straight.
Alpha-tested foliage
Cut-out textures used for leaves, grass, hair and fences.
Shimmering and aliasing; hard for upscalers.

Modelling every leaf with triangles would be far too expensive. Instead, a leaf or a clump of grass is a flat card with a picture on it, where the empty parts are cut away. It is cheap, but the hard cut-out edges alias and shimmer, which is why foliage is so often the least stable part of an image.
Dithering
A pixel pattern used to fake transparency or blend, e.g. on hair or LOD fades.
Visible grain or mesh patterns, worse at low resolution.

True transparency is expensive, so games fake it by drawing only some of an object’s pixels in a checker or noise pattern. Temporal anti-aliasing then blends the pattern into a smooth fade. When the blending fails, usually at low resolution, you can see the dots. It is common on hair, fur and objects fading in.
Hair strands / hair cards
Strand-based hair (each hair) versus cards (flat strips with hair textures).
Realism versus cost of character hair.

Hair cards are flat strips textured to look like many hairs, layered to form a hairstyle. They are cheap and have been the standard for years. Strand hair simulates thousands of individual hairs that move and catch light realistically. It looks much better but is expensive, and can turn noisy at low resolutions.
Physics / destruction
Objects simulated to move, break or react.
Often cut back to save CPU time.

Physics lets objects fall, collide and break according to rules instead of pre-made animation. It runs mainly on the processor, so heavy destruction can pull the frame rate down even when the graphics chip has room to spare. It is one of the few things that can’t be fixed by lowering resolution.
Cloth simulation
Real-time movement of clothing and fabric.
Whether it moves naturally or clips.

Capes, coats, flags and skirts are simulated so they swing and fold with movement and wind. It adds a lot of life to characters. It is sometimes run at half the frame rate to save processing time, and DF points it out when a 60fps game has clothing that visibly moves at 30.
Object / crowd density
How many objects or NPCs fill a scene.
Reduced on weaker platforms.

This is how full the world feels: pedestrians, traffic, clutter, vegetation. Every extra object needs processor time to manage and graphics time to draw. Ports to weaker hardware often thin out crowds and traffic first. Cyberpunk 2077’s emptier streets on PS4 and Switch 2 are a well-known example.

glossary.name: Post-processing & effects
glossary.intro: Post-processing is applied to the finished frame, like a filter. DF judges quality and whether you can turn effects off.
terms: Post-processing
Effects applied after the frame is rendered.
Resolution and quality of each effect.

Once the 3D scene is drawn, the game treats it like a photo and applies filters: blur, glow, color adjustments, grain. These effects give a game much of its cinematic look. They are fairly cheap, and many can be turned off in the options if you prefer a cleaner picture.
Motion blur (camera)
Blur when the whole camera moves.
Often a personal-preference toggle.

When you turn the camera, the whole image is smeared in the direction of movement, imitating a film camera. At 30fps it helps hide the gaps between frames and makes motion look smoother. Many players dislike it because it reduces clarity, so DF appreciates a toggle or a strength slider.
Per-object motion blur
Blur on individual fast-moving objects, like a swinging sword.
DF usually praises it; it smooths low frame rates.

Instead of blurring the whole screen, this blurs only what is moving quickly, such as a sword swing, a spinning wheel or a running character’s limbs. The background stays sharp. It makes animation look smoother and more natural, and it is generally considered the higher-quality form of motion blur.
Depth of field (DOF)
Blurring what's out of focus, like a camera lens.
Quality of edges and bokeh.

Real cameras can only focus at one distance, so things nearer or further are blurred. Games copy this to direct your eye, mainly in cutscenes and when aiming. High-quality versions are expensive, which is one reason cutscenes sometimes run at a lower frame rate or resolution than gameplay.
Bokeh
The shape and look of out-of-focus highlights.
Good bokeh shows proper circles, not smears.

When a bright point of light is out of focus, a real lens turns it into a soft disc or polygon. Good depth of field in games reproduces those shapes, especially for city lights at night. Cheaper versions just smear the background evenly, which looks less like a photograph.
Bloom
Glow spilling from bright lights.
Overdone bloom washes out the image.

Very bright things, such as the sun, lamps or sparks, bleed light into the pixels around them. It mimics how cameras and eyes react to intense light and helps things look bright on a screen with limited brightness. Overdone, it washes out the picture, a look common in games from the mid-2000s.
Chromatic aberration (CA)
Color fringing at screen edges imitating cheap lenses.
Often criticised as unnecessary blur.

A cheap lens splits light slightly, so edges near the corners of a photo pick up red and blue fringes. Some games add this on purpose for a filmed look. It reduces sharpness toward the screen edges, and DF generally prefers it to be optional because it works against a clean image.
Film grain
Added noise imitating film.
Can hide detail and confuse upscalers.

A layer of fine moving noise is added over the picture. It can make a game look more like film and helps hide color banding in dark areas. It also makes the image look noisier and can interfere with video compression, so many players, and DF, like having the choice to switch it off.
Vignette
Darkening toward the screen edges.
Mostly stylistic.

The corners of the image are darkened slightly, as happens with real camera lenses. It subtly draws attention to the centre of the screen. It is a mild effect, and you usually only notice it on bright, even scenes such as snow or sky.
Lens flare
Light streaks and rings from bright sources.
Stylistic.

When a bright light is in view, reflections inside a camera lens create streaks, rings and coloured spots. Games add these to make the sun and bright lamps feel intense. It is purely a stylistic choice, since your eyes don’t see the world that way.
Tone mapping
Converting the scene's brightness range into what a screen can show.
Crushed blacks or blown highlights.

A game calculates light across a huge range, from deep shadow to direct sunlight. A screen can only show a small part of that. Tone mapping compresses the range to fit. Done badly, bright areas turn into flat white or shadows lose detail. It matters most for HDR, where each TV has different limits.
Color grading
The overall color look applied to the image.
Changes between platforms or patches.

Like a film, a game’s final image is adjusted for mood: cool and blue for a night scene, warm and yellow for a desert, washed out for a bleak setting. It is an artistic decision, not a technical one, but DF comments when a remaster changes the grade and alters the feel of the original.
Eye adaptation / auto exposure
The image brightening or darkening as you move between light and dark areas.
Speed and realism of the adjustment.

Walk out of a dark cave and the screen is blindingly bright for a moment before settling, the way your eyes or a camera would adjust. This lets a game show both dark interiors and bright exteriors convincingly. If it reacts too slowly or too strongly, scenes look too dark or blown out.
Particles
Small effects like sparks, smoke, dust and debris.
Density and resolution, often cut on consoles.

Sparks, smoke, dust, rain, magic and debris are each made of many small pieces. A big explosion can put thousands on screen at once. Because they overlap and are often see-through, they are a classic cause of frame rate drops in combat. Returnal and Astro Bot are known for using huge numbers of them smoothly.
Alpha effects / transparencies
Smoke, fire, glass, water and other see-through effects.
Often rendered at low resolution, looking blocky.

See-through effects are expensive because the graphics chip must draw what is behind them and then blend each layer on top. Several overlapping layers of smoke or fire multiply the work. This is why frame rates often fall during explosions, and why these effects are a standard stress test in DF videos.
Half / quarter-resolution effects
Effects rendered at a fraction of the main resolution.
Visible blockiness on smoke, fog and reflections.

To save power, a game can draw smoke, reflections or fog at half or a quarter of the screen resolution and then enlarge them. It usually goes unnoticed because those effects are soft anyway. The giveaway is blocky or jagged edges where the effect crosses a sharp object, like a character standing in front of smoke.
Volumetric clouds
3D clouds that light passes through.
Movement and quality of skies.

Older games painted clouds onto a dome around the world. Volumetric clouds are real 3D shapes that the sun shines through, that cast shadows on the ground, and that you can fly through. They change with weather and time of day. Horizon Forbidden West and Microsoft Flight Simulator are well-known examples.
Water simulation / caustics
Moving water surfaces and the light patterns they cast below.
Realism of water and reflections.

Water is one of the hardest things to draw convincingly. The game has to handle waves, reflections, what you see beneath the surface, and foam. Caustics are the rippling light patterns on a pool floor or a ship’s hull. DF often uses water as a quick test of a game’s rendering quality.
Decals
Textures stamped onto surfaces, like bullet holes or graffiti.
How long they persist.

Decals are small images projected onto existing surfaces: bullet holes, blood, scorch marks, puddles, posters, road markings. They add detail and variety without needing unique textures for every wall. Persistent decals, like bullet holes that stay, also show how much a game remembers about what you did.
Screen-space effects
Any effect using only what's on screen (SSR, SSAO, screen-space shadows).
Breaks at screen edges or behind objects.

These effects use the finished image as their only source of information. That makes them cheap, because the data is already there. They all share one flaw: anything off-screen or hidden behind something can’t contribute. Reflections vanish at screen edges, and shading disappears when an object blocks the view.

glossary.name: Display & latency
glossary.intro: How frames reach your screen and how quickly the game responds to your controller.
terms: Refresh rate (Hz)
How many times per second the display redraws: 60Hz, 120Hz, 144Hz.
Whether the game's frame rate fits the screen.

This is a property of the screen, not the game. A 60Hz TV redraws 60 times a second and can’t show more than 60fps, however fast the console is. A 120Hz TV can show up to 120fps, and it also makes 40fps modes possible. Most recent TVs and the Switch 2’s own screen support 120Hz.
V-sync
Makes the game wait for the display's refresh before showing a new frame.
Stops tearing but can add latency and judder.

With v-sync on, the game holds each finished frame until the screen is ready to start a new refresh, so you never see two frames at once. The cost is that a frame which just misses the deadline has to wait for the next one. That adds a little input delay, and in some games it makes a small drop below 60 fall straight to 30.
Screen tearing
A horizontal split line when a frame changes mid-refresh.
Especially at the top of the screen in console games.

A screen draws its picture from top to bottom. If the game hands over a new frame partway through, the top of the screen shows the old frame and the bottom shows the new one, with a visible line where they meet. It is most obvious when the camera turns. Games allow tearing to avoid the extra delay that v-sync adds.
Adaptive v-sync
V-sync on at target frame rate, off (allowing tearing) below it.
A compromise many console games use.

This is a compromise. While the game hits its target, v-sync stays on and the picture is clean. When it falls below, v-sync switches off so frames are shown immediately. You get some tearing during drops, but you avoid the heavier stutter and input delay that strict v-sync would cause.
Double / triple buffering
Using two or three frame buffers to smooth output.
Triple buffering avoids big drops but adds latency.

With double-buffered v-sync, a frame that misses the screen’s refresh has to wait a whole extra cycle, so a game that can’t quite hold 60 drops straight to 30. Triple buffering adds a spare frame so the game can keep working, which allows in-between rates such as 45 or 50.
VRR (variable refresh rate)
The display matches its refresh to the game's frame rate: G-Sync, FreeSync, HDMI 2.1 VRR.
Makes unlocked or unstable frame rates look smooth.

Normally the TV sets the beat and the game has to keep up. With VRR, the game sets the beat and the TV follows. If a frame takes a bit longer, the screen simply waits for it, so small drops don’t cause tearing or judder. It only works inside a certain range, often 48 to 120Hz, so it can’t fix a game that falls very low.
VRR window
The frame-rate range where VRR works, e.g. 48 to 120Hz.
Drops below the window bring back judder.

A VRR screen can only follow the game within certain limits. On many TVs that range is 48 to 120Hz. If the frame rate falls below the bottom of the window, VRR stops working and you get judder or tearing again. PS5 is known for its narrower window compared with Xbox.
LFC (low framerate compensation)
Doubles frames below the VRR window to keep it working.
Helps games running under 48fps on VRR.

If a game runs at 40fps and the VRR window starts at 48Hz, the system can show every frame twice and run the screen at 80Hz instead. VRR then keeps working at low frame rates. It needs a screen whose top refresh rate is at least double the bottom of its range, which usually means 120Hz.
120Hz mode
Console output at 120Hz, needed for 40fps and 120fps modes.
Whether your TV supports it over HDMI 2.1.

When a console sends 120 pictures a second to the TV, games can offer 120fps modes for very smooth, responsive play, and 40fps modes that divide evenly into 120. It also widens the range in which VRR works. You need a TV with HDMI 2.1 or a 120Hz-capable input to use it.
Input latency / input lag
Delay between pressing a button and seeing the result, in ms.
Frame generation and v-sync add to it.

There is always a short delay between pressing a button and seeing the action. Part of it comes from the game, part from the TV. Higher frame rates reduce it, because each frame arrives sooner. Around 50ms feels sharp; over 100ms starts to feel heavy. It matters most in shooters, fighting games and rhythm games.
End-to-end latency
Total delay from input to the image on screen, also called click-to-photon.
DF's latency tests.

This measures the whole chain: the controller, the game’s processing, the graphics queue, and the TV’s own delay. DF measures it by filming the screen with a high-speed camera and counting the frames between a button press and the first visible reaction. It is the most honest measure of how responsive a game feels.
Nvidia Reflex / AMD Anti-Lag
Tech that cuts input latency by managing the frame queue.
Paired with frame generation to offset its added lag.

Normally the processor prepares frames slightly ahead of the graphics chip, and those waiting frames add delay. These features keep the two in step so frames are drawn with the newest input. The game feels more responsive at the same frame rate. They are PC features, and matter most alongside frame generation.
HDR (high dynamic range)
A wider brightness and color range than SDR.
Real HDR versus fake HDR; peak brightness and blacks.

An HDR picture can show much brighter highlights and deeper shadows at once, with more shades of color. Sunlight, fire and neon can look intense without washing out everything else. How good it looks depends heavily on the TV and on how well the game was set up for it, so results vary a lot.
Nits
Unit of brightness.
HDR highlight targets, e.g. 1000 nits.

A nit is a measure of how bright a screen can get. A standard picture is mastered around 100 nits. Good HDR TVs reach 1,000 or more, and the brightest go beyond 2,000. The Switch 2’s screen reaches roughly 400, which is why DF considers its HDR limited. Game HDR menus often ask for your TV’s peak in nits.
Raised / crushed blacks
Blacks too grey, or dark detail lost.
Common HDR mistakes.

With raised blacks, dark areas look grey and washed out, as if there were a haze over the picture. With crushed blacks, shadows turn solid black and you lose the detail in them. Both usually come from wrong HDR or brightness settings, in the game or the TV, and DF flags games that ship with poor defaults.
HGIG
A TV setting that lets the game handle HDR tone mapping.
Recommended for accurate console HDR.

Normally both the game and the TV try to adjust HDR brightness to fit the screen, and doing it twice gives the wrong result. With HGIG on, the TV steps back and shows exactly what the console sends. You then calibrate once in the console’s HDR setup, and highlights are displayed as the developers intended.
Color banding
Visible steps in smooth gradients like skies.
Low bit depth or compression.

A sunset or a foggy sky should fade smoothly from one shade to the next. If there aren’t enough color steps available, you see distinct stripes. It is most visible in dark scenes and in compressed video. Games hide it with dithering or film grain, and HDR’s extra color depth reduces it.
Motion clarity / persistence
How sharp moving images look on a display.
Why OLED and higher refresh rates look clearer.

Modern flat screens hold each frame still until the next one arrives. As your eye follows a moving object, that held image smears across your vision, so motion looks blurry even though each frame is sharp. Higher frame rates reduce the effect. It is why 120fps looks clearer in motion, not just smoother.
Black frame insertion (BFI)
Inserting black frames to reduce motion blur on displays.
Clearer motion at lower brightness.

The screen flashes each frame briefly and shows black in between. Your eye then sees a short, sharp image instead of a smeared one, so motion looks much clearer. The downsides are a dimmer picture and visible flicker for some people. DF fans of retro games often use it to get a CRT-like look.
CRT
Old tube TVs and monitors with excellent motion clarity.
A DF favourite, especially in John Linneman's retro content.

A CRT draws the picture with a moving beam, so each point lights up for only an instant. That gives extremely clear motion with no smearing. CRTs also handle low resolutions gracefully, which is why older games were designed around them. DF, John Linneman especially, often uses them to show retro games at their best.
Scanlines
The horizontal-line look of CRT images, often recreated with filters.
Accuracy of retro presentation.

On a CRT, a low-resolution image is drawn as separate horizontal lines with thin dark gaps between them. Artists for older games relied on that to blend and soften pixels. On a modern screen the same games look blocky, so retro collections and emulators offer filters that recreate the lines.

glossary.name: Hardware & platforms
glossary.intro: When DF says a game is CPU-limited or GPU-limited, they mean which part of the machine is holding the frame rate back.
terms: CPU
Main processor. Runs game logic, AI, physics, streaming and sends draw work to the GPU.
Busy cities and big crowds lean on it.

The CPU runs everything that isn’t drawing: enemy behaviour, physics, loading data, tracking the world, and preparing the list of things for the graphics chip to draw. If it can’t finish that work in time, the frame rate drops no matter how low the resolution goes. Busy cities and big crowds are typical CPU-heavy scenes.
GPU
Graphics processor; draws the image.
Resolution, lighting and effects lean on it.

The GPU turns the scene into pixels. Its workload grows with resolution and with the quality of lighting, shadows and effects. That is why lowering resolution or switching to a performance mode raises the frame rate: the graphics chip simply has fewer or simpler pixels to produce.
Bottleneck
The component limiting performance.
Which part to upgrade or which setting to lower.

A game needs both the processor and the graphics chip to finish their work for every frame. Whichever one takes longer sets the frame rate, and the other sits partly idle. Identifying which one it is tells you what would actually help: lower settings and resolution for the graphics chip, or nothing much for the processor.
CPU-bound / CPU-limited
Frame rate held back by the CPU; lowering resolution won't help.
Common in open-world and simulation-heavy scenes.

When the processor is the limit, the graphics chip is waiting for instructions. Dropping the resolution makes no difference, which is why some games run poorly in both performance and quality modes. Dragon’s Dogma 2’s crowded cities and Baldur’s Gate 3’s third act are examples DF often cites.
GPU-bound / GPU-limited
Frame rate held back by the GPU; lowering resolution or settings helps.
Most graphics-heavy scenes.

This is the more common and more fixable case on consoles. The graphics chip is working flat out, so reducing resolution, turning down effects or using an upscaler raises the frame rate. Dynamic resolution exists precisely to handle moments like this automatically.
Single-thread performance
How fast one CPU core runs.
Many engines still rely on one main thread.

Many parts of a game have to run in order on one core and can’t be split across several. So the speed of a single core often matters more than how many cores there are. It is the main reason newer processors run games faster, and why the PS5 Pro, with nearly the same CPU as the PS5, can’t fix CPU-limited games.
Main thread / render thread
Key CPU threads running game logic and preparing draw calls.
If one maxes out, the whole game slows.

The main thread runs the game’s core logic in sequence, and the render thread prepares the instructions for the graphics chip. If either is overloaded, the whole game waits, even if other cores are free. Much of the stutter DF finds in Unreal Engine games comes from too much work landing on these threads.
Draw calls
CPU instructions telling the GPU to draw something.
Too many can bottleneck the CPU.

Each separate object or material needs its own instruction from the processor to the graphics chip. Thousands of them per frame add up to real processor time. Scenes full of distinct objects can therefore be CPU-heavy even when they look simple. Newer graphics interfaces such as DirectX 12 and Vulkan reduced this cost.
VRAM
The GPU's own memory.
8GB GPUs struggle in modern games at high texture settings.

This memory holds textures, models and the images the graphics chip is working on. If a game needs more than is available, it has to shuffle data in and out, causing stutter, or fall back to blurry textures. On PC it is a common problem for cards with 8GB or less in recent big-budget games.
Memory bandwidth
How fast data moves to and from memory.
Limits resolution and effects, especially on handhelds.

It isn’t only the amount of memory that matters, but how quickly the system can read and write it. Higher resolutions and many see-through effects move enormous amounts of data each frame. The original Switch was held back by this in docked mode, which DF believes caused Breath of the Wild’s docked stutter.
Unified memory
One shared memory pool for CPU and GPU, as in consoles.
Why console ports can need more VRAM on PC.

On a PC, the processor and graphics card each have their own memory. Consoles use one pool that both share, which developers can divide however the game needs. The PS5 has 16GB in total and the Switch 2 has 12GB. It avoids copying data back and forth, but everything has to fit in the one budget.
TFLOPS
Rough measure of GPU compute power. Series S is about 4, PS5 about 10.3, Series X about 12.
Rough comparisons only; architecture matters.

It counts how many trillion calculations a graphics chip can do per second. It was widely used to compare consoles, but it only compares fairly between chips of the same design. A newer chip does more useful work per TFLOP, so the number says less than it seems, and DF treats it with caution.
Compute units (CUs) / SMs
GPU building blocks on AMD (CUs) and Nvidia (SMs).
More units means more parallel work.

These are the repeated blocks that make up a graphics chip. More of them means more work done at once. The PS5 has 36 compute units and the PS5 Pro has 60, which is where most of its extra graphics power comes from. Leaks and spec sheets often quote these counts.
Clock speed
How fast a chip runs, in MHz or GHz.
Variable clocks on PS5 and handhelds.

A higher clock speed means a chip does more steps per second, at the cost of more power and heat. The Switch and Switch 2 lower their clocks in handheld mode to save battery, which is why games run at lower resolution there. It only compares meaningfully between chips of the same design.
RDNA
AMD's GPU architecture family used in PS5, Xbox Series and Radeon cards.
Feature support like hardware RT.

RDNA is the name for AMD’s recent generations of graphics technology. The PS5 and Xbox Series consoles use a chip based on RDNA 2, the first with ray-tracing support. The PS5 Pro takes parts from later generations, with faster ray tracing. Each generation does more work for the same power.
Tensor cores / AI accelerators
Hardware for machine-learning tasks like DLSS and PSSR.
Why DLSS needs an RTX GPU.

These are parts of a chip built to run neural networks quickly. They are what make AI upscaling practical in real time. Nvidia’s chips, including the one in Switch 2, have them for DLSS. The PS5 Pro added custom hardware for PSSR. The standard PS5 has none, so it relies on non-AI upscalers.
RT cores
Dedicated ray-tracing hardware.
Strength of RT performance per platform.

Finding what a ray hits is slow on ordinary graphics hardware. RT cores are dedicated circuits that do that one job much faster. Nvidia’s are generally stronger than AMD’s equivalent in the PS5 and Xbox, which is one reason console ray tracing is more limited than on a high-end PC.
SSD / NVMe
Fast storage.
Faster loading and streaming on PS5, Series X and PC.

A solid-state drive has no moving parts and reads data many times faster than the hard drives in PS4 and Xbox One. Loading drops from a minute to a few seconds, and games can pull in new areas quickly enough to remove loading corridors and most texture pop-in. NVMe is the fast connection type these drives use.
Hardware decompression
Dedicated chips unpacking game data (PS5's Kraken unit, Xbox Velocity Architecture).
Fast streaming without loading the CPU.

Game data is stored compressed to save space, and unpacking it used to tie up the processor during loading. The PS5 and Xbox Series consoles have dedicated hardware that does the unpacking, leaving the processor free. That is a large part of why loading on them is so much faster than a PC with a similar drive.
DirectStorage
Windows API for faster loading from NVMe drives.
Load times and streaming on PC.

DirectStorage brings the consoles’ fast-loading approach to Windows. It cuts the overhead of reading many small files from a fast drive and can use the graphics card to unpack data. Few games use it fully so far. Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart and Forspoken were early examples.
TDP / power draw
How much power a chip uses, in watts.
Key for Steam Deck and Switch 2; affects battery and clocks.

Power use is the hard limit on performance. A home console can draw around 200 watts; a handheld runs on 10 to 20. That gap, more than anything else, explains the difference between PS5 and Switch 2 results. DF often measures power at the wall to compare how efficiently machines run the same game.
Thermal throttling
A chip slowing down when too hot.
Laptops and handhelds.

Chips protect themselves by slowing down if they overheat. In a console with good cooling it should never happen. It is a real concern for thin laptops, phones and handheld PCs, where performance can drop after several minutes of play. DF tests long sessions to check for it.
Docked / handheld mode
Switch and Switch 2 run at different power and clocks in each mode.
Resolution and frame-rate differences between modes.

In the dock, the console has mains power and better cooling, so it runs its chips faster and targets a TV. In handheld it slows them to save battery and targets its own smaller screen. Games therefore have two profiles, usually with a lower resolution in handheld, and DF tests both.
PS5 Pro
Upgraded PS5 with a stronger GPU, better RT and PSSR.
PS5 Pro Enhanced patches and how much they add.

Released in November 2024, the Pro has a graphics chip around 45% faster than the standard PS5, stronger ray tracing and the PSSR upscaler. Its processor is almost unchanged. So it delivers sharper images and extra ray-traced effects, but it can’t fix games held back by the processor.
Series S
Xbox's lower-power console with less memory.
Often the weakest version DF tests.

The Series S has a processor close to the Series X but about a third of the graphics power and less memory. Developers must support it, so it often sets the baseline for a game. DF uses it as the closest comparison for Switch 2 ports, since the two land in a similar range when docked.
Steam Deck / handheld PCs
PC handhelds running games at low power.
Playability at 30 to 60fps on low settings.

The Steam Deck runs PC games on a low-power chip at about 800p. It is a useful yardstick for how a game scales down, and DF frequently compares it with Switch 2. The Deck has more raw flexibility; Switch 2 has DLSS and ports tuned specifically for its hardware.
Backwards compatibility
Running older-generation games on new hardware.
Boost modes and FPS Boost upgrades.

The PS5 runs PS4 games and the Switch 2 runs Switch games. Without a patch, they keep their original caps, but anything that used to fall short now runs at its best: steadier frame rates, top dynamic resolution, faster loading. With a patch, developers can raise resolution and frame rate further.
Emulation
Software imitating another system to run its games.
Accuracy and performance of emulated classics.

An emulator makes one machine behave like another, so software written for the old system runs unchanged. It takes far more power than the original hardware had. Nintendo’s classic libraries and many retro collections work this way. DF checks them for accuracy, added input delay and options such as CRT filters.

glossary.name: Ports, engines & show jargon
glossary.intro: Game engines, PC port quality and the shorthand DF uses in videos and on DF Direct.
terms: Game engine
The software foundation a game is built on: Unreal Engine 5, Unity, id Tech, Decima, RE Engine, Frostbite, Snowdrop.
Each has typical strengths and known problems.

An engine provides the common machinery every game needs: drawing, physics, sound, loading, tools for artists. Studios either license one, like Unreal, or build their own, like Decima or RE Engine. The engine shapes a game’s strengths and typical problems, so DF often predicts how a game will behave from which engine it uses.
Unreal Engine 5 (UE5)
Epic's engine with Nanite, Lumen and TSR.
Great visuals, frequent stutter, heavy performance demands.

Unreal Engine 5 is now the most widely used engine for big-budget games. Its headline features are Nanite for geometry, Lumen for lighting and TSR for upscaling. They allow very detailed worlds, but they are demanding. Low internal resolutions and traversal stutter are common DF complaints about UE5 games on console.
Port
A version of a game moved to another platform.
Whether it was done carefully or rushed.

Porting means adapting a game to hardware it wasn’t originally built for. The work ranges from light adjustments to deep rewrites when the target is much weaker, as with Switch 2 versions of PS5 games. DF judges a port on what was cut, what was kept, and how well it runs on the new machine.
PC port quality
How well a PC version runs and what options it offers.
Stutter, settings menu, scaling and bugs.

A good PC version runs smoothly, has no shader stutter, supports different screen shapes and input devices, and gives players a full set of graphics options. A bad one stutters on powerful hardware or lacks basic settings. Alex Battaglia’s PC reviews at DF focus heavily on these points.
Optimised settings
DF's recommended PC settings: near-max quality at much lower cost.
Usually Alex Battaglia's segment.

Maximum settings on PC often cost a lot of performance for improvements you can barely see. DF tests each option, finds where the visible benefit stops, and publishes a recommended list. Following it typically gives a large frame rate gain over maximum settings with almost no visible loss.
Console-equivalent settings
PC settings matching what PS5 or Xbox uses.
Shows how a given PC compares to consoles.

By comparing footage closely, DF works out which PC options match what the PS5 or Xbox version uses. It shows what consoles are really running, often a mix of medium and high. It also lets PC players with similar hardware copy a configuration the developers already judged to be well balanced.
Scalability
How well a game runs across weak and strong hardware.
Low settings that actually help performance.

A scalable game or engine can be turned down far enough to run on a handheld and turned up far enough to challenge a top PC, while still looking like the same game. It is why some games get impressive Switch 2 or Steam Deck versions and others can’t be brought across without heavy cuts.
Graphics options menu
The PC settings available.
DF praises previews, explanations and VRAM meters.

DF looks at how many settings a PC game offers, whether they are explained, and whether changes can be previewed without restarting. A good menu shows what each option does and how much it costs. Missing basics, like an upscaler choice or a field-of-view slider, count against a port.
Day-one patch
An update released at launch.
Whether launch issues get fixed.

Discs are finished weeks before release, and developers keep fixing things in the meantime. The day-one patch delivers those fixes. It can change performance a lot, so DF notes which version it tested, and sometimes revisits a game once the patch is out.
Remaster / remake
A remaster updates the original; a remake rebuilds it from scratch.
How faithful and how improved.

A remaster keeps the original game and its code, and improves resolution, frame rate, textures and sometimes lighting. A remake is built again from nothing, with new models and often new gameplay. Some releases sit in between. DF compares them with the original to show exactly what changed.
Next-gen / Pro patch
An update adding modes for newer hardware.
Real upgrade versus a simple resolution bump.

Games released for older or base hardware often get an update later that adds higher resolution, a 60fps mode, or ray tracing on newer machines. PS5 Pro patches and Switch 2 Editions are recent examples. DF checks whether the patch is a real upgrade or only a small resolution bump.
Side-by-side / head-to-head
Footage of two platforms or modes played together.
DF's main comparison format.

DF captures the same scene on two machines or in two modes and shows them together, either split down the middle or one after the other. It is the clearest way to reveal differences in sharpness, lighting or detail. DF often zooms in, because many differences are invisible at normal viewing distance.
Frame-time graph
The line under DF footage showing each frame's time in ms.
A flat line is smooth; spikes are stutter.
