The graph plots how long every frame took. A flat line means consistent delivery. A spike means one frame stayed on screen too long, which you feel as a stutter. It reveals problems that an average fps number hides, and it is one of the defining tools of DF’s videos.
Stress point
The heaviest scene used to see how low performance goes.
Worst-case performance.

Most of a game runs fine. DF goes looking for the scenes that don’t: the busiest city, the largest battle, the effect-heavy boss. Those show the worst case you will meet. A game that holds up in its stress points can be trusted everywhere else.
Like-for-like
A comparison using matched settings and scenes.
Fair platform comparisons.

For a fair comparison, everything except the thing being tested has to match: the same scene, the same settings, the same moment. If one console is shown in quality mode and the other in performance mode, the result is meaningless. DF uses this phrase to signal that it has controlled for those differences.
Capture card
Hardware recording raw video output for analysis.
Lets DF measure frame rate and tearing from the signal.

DF records exactly what the console outputs, with no extra compression, using capture hardware connected by HDMI. Its own analysis software then examines every frame to find duplicates and tears, which produces the frame rate and frame-time readouts. Handheld screens can’t be captured this way, which is why handheld tests are sometimes estimates.
FPS Boost
Xbox feature that doubles frame rates of older games.
Free backwards-compatibility upgrades.

Xbox Series consoles can run certain older games at double their original frame rate, 60 instead of 30 or 120 instead of 60, with no patch from the developer. It works at the system level. DF covered it extensively because it transformed how many Xbox One games feel.
Tech analysis
DF's in-depth video breaking down how a game works and runs.
Their main content type.

This is DF’s core format. A reviewer measures resolution and frame rate, examines the lighting, detail and effects, compares platforms and modes, and gives a recommendation on how best to play. It doesn’t score the game’s design or story. The reviews in this app summarise these analyses.
DF Direct
DF's weekly discussion show with Richard Leadbetter, John Linneman, Alex Battaglia, Oliver Mackenzie and others.
News, Q&A and opinions.

DF Direct Weekly is the team’s discussion show and podcast. They react to the week’s gaming and hardware news, talk about upcoming tests, and answer supporter questions. It is looser than their analysis videos and a good place to hear the terms in this dictionary used in conversation.
Jank
Informal term for rough, buggy or unpolished behaviour.
Broken animations, odd physics, strange glitches.

Jank covers the small rough edges that don’t break a game but make it feel unfinished: stiff animation, odd physics, camera hiccups, textures that load late. DF uses it affectionately for ambitious games that are rough around the edges, and critically for big releases that should be more polished.
Temporal stability
How stable an image stays from frame to frame in motion.
No flicker, fizzle or crawling.

A screenshot can look sharp while the moving game shimmers and flickers. Temporal stability describes how well the picture holds together over time: edges that don’t crawl, foliage that doesn’t sparkle, reflections that don’t flicker. It is one of the main things separating good upscalers from poor ones.
Soft / blurry image
An image lacking sharpness, often from low resolution or heavy TAA.
A common console criticism.

A soft image looks slightly out of focus, as if seen through a thin film. The usual causes are a low internal resolution stretched to fit the screen, heavy temporal anti-aliasing, or an upscaler pushed too far. It is one of DF’s most common criticisms of performance modes.
Clean presentation
A sharp, stable, artifact-free image.
High praise.

This is high praise from DF. It means the picture is sharp, edges are smooth, nothing flickers or ghosts, and the frame rate is steady. Nintendo’s best games and Sony’s first-party titles often earn it. It usually reflects careful choices more than raw power.
Next-gen / current-gen / cross-gen
New hardware generation; games built for it; or games released on old and new consoles.
Whether old hardware limited the design.

Cross-gen games are released on both the old and new consoles, so they have to be designed around the older hardware’s limits. That held back many early PS5 games. Current-gen-only games drop the old consoles and can rely on fast storage and stronger processors, which usually shows in their scale and detail.
Generational leap
A big visual jump only possible on new hardware.
Rarely awarded.

DF uses this for visuals that clearly couldn’t have been done on the previous hardware: far more detailed worlds, ray-traced lighting, instant loading. It is high praise. They also use it for remasters, when a new version looks a full generation ahead of the original.
DF best graphics awards
DF's yearly picks for the most technically impressive games.
The standout tech of the year.

At the end of each year the DF team discusses and ranks the games that impressed them most technically. They weigh visual ambition, performance and polish across PC and consoles. The lists are a useful way to find the standout showcases from any given year.

reviews.headline: ~40fps base · 60fps with frame generation
reviews.overview: DF called it a better than expected Switch 2 port with gentler compromises than many recent ones. The game's key lighting is intact, and it reaches 60 frames per second only with frame generation.

findings.text: Without help the game hovers around 40 frames per second. The 60fps option uses [[frame generation|Frame generation]] to create the extra frames from that [[base frame rate|Base frame rate]]. DF called this not a bad choice given the hardware, but felt a proper [[40fps mode|40fps mode]] might have been the better experience.
The key lighting systems were kept, so the game keeps its visual character. DF noted Stellar Blade's visuals were always fairly conservative, which made it easier to bring across.
The cuts are mostly small downgrades to models and textures that you would only spot in a side-by-side comparison with PS5.

reviews.game: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
reviews.headline: 1440p · locked 60fps · FSR
reviews.overview: John Linneman calls this remake one of Nintendo's best efforts on Switch 2, both in how it looks and how it runs. His criticisms are minor, and the jump from the N64 original, which ran at roughly 20 frames per second, is enormous.

findings.text: The game runs at a [[locked|Locked / capped]] 60 frames per second in both docked and handheld play, and it stays there consistently. The only blemishes DF spotted were very small [[hitches|Stutter / hitch]] while the game loads new areas in the background, which most players are unlikely to notice.

Resolution changes on the fly to keep performance steady, a technique called [[dynamic resolution scaling|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]]. Docked, it moves between 1080p and 1440p, and handheld between 720p and 1080p. Nintendo appears to upscale the image with AMD's [[FSR]] rather than Nvidia's [[DLSS]], which the Switch 2 has dedicated hardware for, and that choice leaves some [[shimmering|Shimmering / specular aliasing]] on fine detail like foliage and thin edges.

Lighting is one of the highlights. DF singled out the [[atmospheric fog|Volumetric lighting / fog]] that hangs in many environments, and the glowing lava in the Fire Temple, which actually [[lights the scene around it|Emissive lighting]] rather than just looking bright.

Handheld mode makes a few extra cuts to hold 60fps on a smaller power budget. Objects switch to simpler [[level-of-detail|Level of detail (LOD)]] models closer to the camera, and some [[textures|Texture resolution]] are lower resolution than in docked play.

reviews.headline: 1440p/30 or 900–1080p/60 · avoid 40fps
reviews.overview: DF found Phantom Blade Zero a respectable release on both PlayStation consoles, and recommends the 60fps Performance mode on either. The 40fps Balanced mode is the main flaw: its frame rate is too uneven to recommend.

findings.text: Performance mode holds 60 frames per second well, which suits the fast combat. The 40fps Balanced mode, aimed at 120Hz and [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] TVs, has significant [[frame-rate inconsistencies|Frame pacing]] on both the standard PS5 and the PS5 Pro, so DF advises against it until the developers fix it.

On the standard PS5, Graphics mode renders a [[native|Native resolution]] 1440p at 30fps, and Performance mode moves [[dynamically|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] between 900p and 1080p. The PS5 Pro looks noticeably sharper in every mode because it uses [[PSSR]] instead of the standard upscaler.
The PS5 Pro adds a toggle for hardware [[ray-traced reflections|RT reflections]] on mirrors and water, but DF found it makes virtually no difference during actual play.

reviews.headline: 60fps target · dips to 50s and 40s
reviews.overview: DF found a range of downgrades from the PS5 version, leaving the Switch 2 port looking closer to PS4. It targets 60 frames per second and mostly holds it, with drops in busy fights.

modes.fps: 60 target, dips to 50s, 40s in set pieces

findings.text: The game targets 60 frames per second and mostly gets there, dipping into the 50s in busier moments and into the 40s in some combat set pieces. DF suggested a locked [[40fps mode|40fps mode]] would have been a good option.
Some lights no longer cast real-time shadows, some reflections are missing, and the [[volumetric lighting|Volumetric lighting / fog]] is coarser, with larger, blurrier light shafts than on PS5.
[[Texture resolution|Texture resolution]] is roughly on par with PS5, but foliage is less dense and distant enemies use [[half-rate animation|Half-rate animation]].
DF also looked briefly at Resident Evil 2 and 3 on Switch 2. Those were built for PS4, so they hold up better and run at a more consistent 60.

reviews.headline: PS5 Pro 80–90fps or 60fps RT
reviews.overview: DF calls The Witcher 3 Remastered a visually impressive benchmark with advanced lighting, and says the PS5 Pro is easily the best place to play it on console. After patch 5.01 it runs better everywhere, though there is still room for improvement.

findings.text: After patch 5.01, frame rates improved across the board, with smoother play in busy areas and demanding cutscenes, though slight dips remain. The standard PS5 version is described as pretty solid. On PS5 Pro with a 120Hz display, Performance mode typically runs at 80 to 90 frames per second.
Without a [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] display, [[screen tearing|Screen tearing]] can still appear.

The PS5 Pro uses [[PSSR]]. Its ray-tracing mode renders at a lower internal resolution and can look softer than the standard PS5 in still scenes, but DF saw almost no difference during actual play, and that's the mode they recommend for its visual upgrades.
[[Bloom]] is overused and can wash out environmental detail. The patch added an option to reduce it on console, and DF suggests using it.

reviews.headline: 540p–1080p docked DLSS · 40fps cap (30 recommended)
reviews.overview: DF called the Switch 2 version a huge upgrade over the original Switch release, with reworked lighting, better textures and less pop-in. The new 40 frames per second cap can't be held everywhere, so DF recommends playing at 30.

findings.text: On a 120Hz screen the game offers a [[40fps cap|40fps mode]]. It holds up in quieter open areas but isn't sustainable in busier ones, so DF recommends the 30fps cap, which stays stable. On a 60Hz TV the cap drops to 30 anyway. The original Switch version often fell into the 20s.

Both modes use [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] with [[DLSS|DLSS]]: 540p to 1080p docked and 360p to 720p handheld. When resolution drops, [[screen-space reflections|Screen-space reflections (SSR)]] and cutscene [[depth of field|Depth of field (DOF)]] suffer most.
The lighting is reworked, local lights now cast dynamic shadows, and [[ambient occlusion|Ambient occlusion (AO)]] is more precise. There is no [[ray tracing|Ray tracing (RT)]] on Switch 2.

[[Textures|Texture resolution]] are higher quality, grass and plants are shaded better, and improved [[level of detail|Level of detail (LOD)]] means less [[pop-in|Pop-in]] than on Switch 1. The download grows from about 39GB to 55.5GB.

reviews.headline: 720p→1440p · locked 30fps
reviews.overview: DF sees Fortune's Weave as a clear technical step up from Fire Emblem Engage. It is clean, stable and quick to load, but the choice to stick with 30 frames per second, with no 60fps option, is a little disappointing on hardware this capable.

findings.text: The game is [[locked|Locked / capped]] to 30 frames per second, and DF found no drops at all, so it is very consistent. The trade-off is that motion is less smooth than in Nintendo games that run at 60, like Mario Kart World, which you notice most when the camera pans across the map.

The game renders at a [[base resolution|Internal / base resolution]] of 720p when docked and 540p in handheld, then [[reconstructs|Temporal upscaling / reconstruction]] the image up to 1440p and 1080p respectively. DF thinks Nvidia's [[DLSS]] may be doing that reconstruction, but couldn't confirm it.

Textures and shadows are fine for the style. Some surfaces look a little blurry when seen at an angle, which points to modest [[texture filtering|Anisotropic filtering (AF)]], but it never becomes distracting. Moving between areas is quick, helped by the Switch 2's faster [[storage|SSD / NVMe]].

reviews.headline: 864p · 60fps · rough image
reviews.overview: Control Resonant has a rough start on PlayStation. The standard PS5 struggles with low resolution, shimmering and frame-rate drops, and the PS5 Pro improves things without fully fixing them. DF thinks post-launch patches could help, and wonders whether Remedy's Northlight engine is a good fit for a more open world.

findings.text: On a standard PS5, Performance mode targets 60fps and mostly gets close, but [[traversal stutter|Traversal stutter]] appears when moving quickly, and melee attacks during the first boss cause dips. Quality mode targets 30fps and falls into the 20s in that same fight. The PS5 Pro's Performance mode holds 60 more steadily, while its [[Balanced mode]] at 40fps is the least consistent of the three.

Performance mode on PS5 renders at just 864p and uses AMD's [[FSR]] to upscale to 1440p, which leaves obvious [[shimmering|Shimmering / specular aliasing]] and artifacts. Quality mode upscales from 1260p to 4K and looks much sharper. On PS5 Pro, the same 864p base is reconstructed all the way to 4K using [[PSSR]], which is a clear improvement, though image quality still isn't where DF would like it.

Ray tracing is only available on PS5 Pro. Its Quality mode adds [[ray-traced reflections|RT reflections]] and [[ray-traced shadows|RT shadows]], which noticeably improve shadow definition. On the standard PS5, longer views reveal low-resolution [[shadows|Shadow maps]].
DF expects patches to improve things. They also raise the question of whether Remedy's [[engine|Game engine]], which was built for tighter, more linear games, is well suited to this more open design.

findings.title: QSSR on standard PS5 (November 2026)
findings.text: Remedy plans to add [[QSSR]], Sony's AI upscaler for the standard PS5, in a December 2026 update. Remedy says it makes the image much more stable and detailed. This is the developer's description; DF hasn't tested it yet.

reviews.headline: 1440p→4K · 60fps · PSSR on Pro
reviews.overview: DF calls Marvel's Wolverine a superbly crafted adventure that plays well on a standard PS5 but is at its best on PS5 Pro. Both consoles hold their frame-rate targets almost perfectly, and DF recommends the 60fps Performance mode on either machine. The main technical limitation is lighting, which still relies on older techniques instead of full ray-traced global illumination.

findings.text: Both consoles hold their targets with only minimal dips during camera transitions, so the game feels consistent whichever mode you choose. On a 120Hz TV, the PS5 Pro's Fidelity mode can run at a [[40fps mode|40fps mode]], and with [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] and the frame rate unlocked, Performance mode climbs to around 70 to 80fps, while Fidelity sits around 40 to 50.

On PS5 Pro, Performance mode renders at around 1440p and uses Sony's AI upscaler, [[PSSR]], to reconstruct a 4K image. That means Pro owners don't have to choose between smoothness and sharpness. On a standard PS5, Performance mode averages around 1296p and uses Insomniac's own temporal upscaler, IGTI. It looks noticeably softer, with visible artifacts and [[jagged edges|Aliasing / jaggies]], so base PS5 owners face a real trade-off between 60fps and a clean image. Fidelity mode renders at around 1800p on both consoles and is much sharper, at 30fps.

[[Ray-traced reflections|RT reflections]] are clean on both consoles. The PS5 Pro's Fidelity mode can add extra ray tracing, including [[ray-traced ambient occlusion|RTAO]], which removes the obvious mistakes that cheaper [[screen-space ambient occlusion|SSAO / HBAO / GTAO]] makes in corners and creases. The weakness is indirect lighting. Instead of [[ray-traced global illumination|RTGI]], the game uses an older system of [[light probes|Light probes]] combined with screen-space effects, which leaves some areas lit with no obvious light source. The upside is that you never see the grainy, noisy ray-traced lighting that some other console games suffer from.

Shadows use traditional [[cascaded shadow maps|Cascaded shadow maps (CSM)]], so you can see them [[pop in|Pop-in]] and change detail as the camera moves, and small objects lose fine shadow detail. The Pro's Fidelity mode improves shadow sharpness, [[level of detail|Level of detail (LOD)]] and the animation of vegetation.
DF singles out the blood effects and the amount of environmental [[destruction|Physics / destruction]] as highlights that make combat feel brutal and physical.

findings.title: QSSR on standard PS5 (October 2026)
findings.text: Wolverine was one of the first games DF tested with [[QSSR]], Sony's new AI upscaler for the standard PS5. Compared with Insomniac's own upscaler, distant trucks, fences and foliage hold more detail, Wolverine's hair is less noisy, water gains detail and loses its [[ghosting|Ghosting / trails]], and the already good [[ray-traced reflections|RT reflections]] improve further. DF called the result exceptional.

findings.title: QSSR: the cost
findings.text: In performance mode QSSR upscales an 864p image to 1440p and costs about 1.5 to 1.8 milliseconds per frame more than the old upscaler, roughly 8 to 10 frames per second at the same resolution. To hold 60, the game lowers its [[internal resolution|Internal / base resolution]] when needed. Upscaling all the way to 4K costs about 4.4 milliseconds, more than twice what [[PSSR]] takes on [[PS5 Pro|PS5 Pro]], so DF sees 1440p as the better target for the standard console.

reviews.headline: 720p–1080p docked / 432p–864p handheld · 30–35fps
reviews.overview: DF called it a successful port that benefited greatly from its delay. It broadly matches the PS4 feature set with better frame rates, higher resolution and much faster loading, though the 40fps cap is rarely reached.

findings.text: The frame rate is capped at 40, but the game can't sustain that for long. Typical play sits at 30 to 35 frames per second in both modes, so it is smoother than PS4 but not steady.
Both modes use [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]]. There is no graphics menu or mode toggle, so the settings are fixed from the moment you start.
Loading is a highlight: it is far faster than on PS4 and Xbox One, which matters in a game where you die and reload often.
DF sees it as the PS4 version improved, not a match for PS5. The original 2025 release was delayed for performance work, and DF felt that time made a big difference.

reviews.headline: Up to 1080p docked / 900p handheld · optional 30fps cap
reviews.overview: DF called this probably Capcom's best Switch 2 release so far, mainly because it offers an optional 30 frames per second cap, something its other Switch 2 ports lacked.

findings.text: You can leave the frame rate [[unlocked|Unlocked]], which DF found perfectly playable, or turn on a 30fps [[cap|Locked / capped]]. The cap gives much more stable gameplay and a slight visual boost.
Docked tops out at 1080p and can dip below it, while handheld reaches 900p. Compared with other platforms the image has noticeably less contrast and sharpness.
Even against PS5 Pro, DF said the Switch 2 version holds up well and delivers the full experience despite its cutbacks.

reviews.headline: PSSR shines on Pro · no ray tracing
reviews.overview: DF calls Resonance a visual feast on every console. The PS5 Pro version is a class apart in image quality, although the Xbox Series X version delivers a tighter frame rate than either PlayStation, for reasons DF couldn't pin down.

findings.text: On PS5 Pro, [[PSSR]] sharpens distant detail like foliage and branches, and greatly reduces the [[shimmer|Shimmering / specular aliasing]] and [[banding|Color banding]] that standard [[TAA|TAA (temporal AA)]] upscaling shows when the camera moves. That's the main reason DF calls the Pro version a class apart.

Across every mode, including the unlocked 120Hz option, the Xbox Series X holds its frame rate more tightly than the PlayStation versions, even at the same resolution targets. DF couldn't determine why.

Asobo built the game on [[Unreal Engine 5|Unreal Engine 5 (UE5)]] but skipped [[ray tracing|Ray tracing (RT)]], which other outlets highlighted as an example of how to keep a UE5 game running well on console.

reviews.game: The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Remastered
reviews.headline: 1080p docked / 900p handheld DLSS · 30fps, poor pacing
reviews.overview: DF found Oblivion Remastered looks impressive on Switch 2, even beating Xbox Series S visually, but called the performance frustrating because of constant camera hitching.

findings.text: The target is 30 frames per second, but [[frame pacing|Frame pacing]] is poor. Frame times flip between 16ms and 50ms, which you see as constant [[hitching|Stutter / hitch]] whenever the camera moves.
[[DLSS|DLSS]] gives a 1080p picture docked and 900p handheld, and DF found the overall visuals better than the [[Series S|Series S]] version.
Foliage is reduced, with entire trees missing from the overworld, and distant objects [[pop in|Pop-in]] and out as you move.

The slowdown that builds up over long sessions on PS5 and Xbox doesn't appear here, probably because of the 30fps cap. The full game also fits on a cartridge, which DF found impressive for an [[Unreal Engine 5|Unreal Engine 5 (UE5)]] game.

reviews.headline: 1440p · locked 60fps · huge enemy counts
reviews.overview: Splatoon Raiders is the first Splatoon built only for Switch 2, and DF calls it a safe but satisfying upgrade. The extra power goes mainly into a sharper image and much bigger enemy hordes at a steady 60 frames per second, while the lighting, textures and engine still feel like an evolution of the Switch era rather than a fresh start.

findings.text: Even in the busiest fights, with crowds of enemies, ink splatter and explosions filling the screen, the game holds a rock-solid 60 frames per second. Cutscenes mostly run at 30fps, occasionally switching to 60, and they can dip when complex water effects appear. DF thinks this much chaos would likely have forced a 30fps cap or heavy cuts on the original Switch, which helps explain why the game is a Switch 2 exclusive.

Docked, the game usually renders at 1440p and only occasionally drops to around 1260p, a big step up from Splatoon 3's 840p to 1080p range on the original Switch. In handheld it renders a [[native|Native resolution]] 1080p that matches the screen exactly. The weak spot is [[anti-aliasing|Anti-aliasing (AA)]]: a custom mobile version of AMD's [[FSR]] combined with [[SMAA|FXAA / SMAA]] reduces the [[shimmer|Shimmering / specular aliasing]] on detailed surfaces like rusted metal and fishnets, but doesn't remove it. In handheld there is no anti-aliasing at all, so edges look visibly [[jagged|Aliasing / jaggies]].

Lighting is [[baked|Baked lighting / lightmaps]], meaning it is calculated ahead of time rather than live, just as in earlier Splatoon games. Water reflections use pre-captured [[cube maps|Cube maps]] instead of [[screen-space reflections|Screen-space reflections (SSR)]], so they don't accurately mirror what's around them.

The most impressive achievement is [[how many enemies|Object / crowd density]] the game can show at once. They are detailed, [[physics-driven|Physics / destruction]] models, and there are far more of them than in Splatoon 3's Salmon Run mode. Elsewhere, [[textures|Texture resolution]] and [[texture filtering|Texture filtering]] are still fairly basic.

The ink itself has some subtle upgrades. Swimming through it creates more dynamic ripples, and shots that hit existing paint now bounce off, which makes the world feel more reactive. Screens packed with [[ink and explosion effects|Alpha effects / transparencies]] don't hurt performance.

Overall, DF describes this as a scaled-up version of the existing [[engine|Game engine]] rather than a rebuild. They were surprised it doesn't support the Joy-Con 2 mouse controls, and hope the next main Splatoon brings both mouse support and a more modern engine.

reviews.headline: 720p internal · 60fps target
reviews.overview: This paid upgrade finally gets Xenoblade Chronicles 2 running close to 60 frames per second, which DF sees as a solid improvement for a game that struggled badly on the original Switch. Image quality is better too, though it still falls well short of a sharp 4K look.

findings.text: The Switch 2 Edition targets 60 frames per second in both modes, while the original often dropped into the 20s during exploration and cutscenes. Small drops remain in effects-heavy cutscenes and in some traversal. Handheld feels slightly smoother than docked, which DF suspects is because the handheld screen supports [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] and can absorb small drops more gracefully.

DF believes the game uses [[double-buffered|Double / triple buffering]] [[v-sync|V-sync]]. With that setup, if the game misses its 16.7 millisecond frame budget several times in a row, it can't show 50 or 55fps, so it falls straight to 30 until things settle. That's why drops feel sharper than the numbers alone suggest.

Docked, the game renders at 720p internally. Most of the improvement comes from [[temporal upscaling|Temporal upscaling / reconstruction]], which builds a sharper image from several frames, and DF suspects a [[spatial upscaler|Spatial upscaling]] is added on top, as in Xenoblade Chronicles X. The downside is visible jitter whenever the camera cuts to a new angle, because the upscaler has no history for the new view, and some textures look soft. Handheld rises to about 468p from 368p on the original Switch, which still beats the original's docked image.

[[Depth of field|Depth of field (DOF)]] has been improved, and there are minor lighting upgrades. Cutscenes with lots of [[transparent effects|Alpha effects / transparencies]] are where the frame rate is most likely to dip.
Grass is [[denser|Object / crowd density]] while you explore, which makes the open areas feel fuller than before.

reviews.game: Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag Resynced
reviews.headline: RTGI · 1440p/30, 1080p/60 · best on Pro
reviews.overview: Oliver Mackenzie calls Black Flag Resynced one of the best remakes ever, and says it even looks better than Assassin's Creed Shadows. Almost everything has been rebuilt, lighting is now fully ray traced, and it runs solidly on every console, with the PS5 Pro the clear pick outside PC.

findings.text: The original game's pre-baked lighting is replaced with full [[ray-traced global illumination|RTGI]], which looks more natural and has fewer artifacts. In Fidelity mode on the standard PS5, the sea also gets [[ray-traced reflections|RT reflections]], rendered at a quarter of the internal resolution. Performance mode drops those reflections and falls back to [[screen-space|Screen-space effects]] shadows.

On the standard PS5, Fidelity mode renders at about 1440p, and the Balanced and Performance modes at 1080p. An improved [[temporal upscaler|Temporal upscaling / reconstruction]] keeps the image clean. The PS5 Pro uses [[PSSR]] 2 to reconstruct a much sharper, less flickery image from the same internal resolution. One bug: importing an old save turns PSSR off on Pro and falls back to the standard upscaler. Starting a new game avoids it until Ubisoft's patch arrives.

The game runs solidly with a generally stable frame rate. The 40fps [[Balanced mode]] needs a 120Hz display and keeps most of Fidelity's settings, which other outlets highlighted as a sweet spot. On PS5 Pro, the 60fps Performance mode keeps the full ray-traced sea reflections and better hair simulation, essentially Fidelity-level visuals at double the frame rate.

Nearly every asset was rebuilt with much denser geometry. Characters were redesigned with advanced skin shading, [[subsurface scattering|Subsurface scattering (SSS)]] and strand-based [[hair|Hair strands / hair cards]] taken from Shadows. A new cloth system simulates clothing and ship sails, though Performance mode on the standard PS5 simplifies hair and sails.
Water is a highlight: sea reflections improve on Shadows, foam is more realistic, light scatters through the water better, and shallow water has [[fluid simulation|Water simulation / caustics]].
This is a full [[remake|Remaster / remake]] of the 2013 game. Most of the original motion capture was kept, with artists fixing it by hand where needed.

reviews.headline: ~1080p · stable 60fps · no stutter
reviews.overview: DF calls the Star Fox remake one of the best-looking games on Switch 2: smooth, polished and beautiful. It keeps the feel of Star Fox 64 while adding modern visuals and real-time cutscenes, and DF sees it as a refined return for both the series and the rail-shooter genre.

findings.text: The game runs at a stable 60 frames per second, double the N64 original's 30, with no [[stutters|Stutter / hitch]] or instability. DF points out that this avoids the performance problems seen in many of the more demanding Switch 2 releases.
Image quality is solid but not spectacular. John Linneman estimates it renders at around 1080p, which looks clean on a TV without being razor-sharp.
On an [[HDR|HDR (high dynamic range)]] TV, bright highlights like lasers and explosions pop nicely. DF didn't analyze the HDR in depth, so they can't yet say whether it is technically perfect.

The game runs on Velan Studios' Viper engine. Materials use [[physically based rendering|Physically based rendering (PBR)]], so metal, glass and rock react to light the way they would in reality, which gives them a convincing sense of weight. [[Volumetric effects|Volumetric lighting / fog]] add depth to space stages, nebula dust and atmospheric planets.

[[Depth of field|Depth of field (DOF)]] and [[motion blur|Motion blur (camera)]] tie the look together into something dramatic and cinematic. Underwater stages have convincing [[caustics|Water simulation / caustics]], the rippling light patterns you see on a sea floor, along with plenty of [[particle effects|Particles]].

[[Draw distances|Draw distance]] are far longer than in the original, so levels feel much bigger. At the same time, enemies are still introduced carefully, so each stage keeps the pacing of Star Fox 64.

This is a full [[remake|Remaster / remake]] rather than a touch-up, with new real-time cutscenes that keep the puppet-like charm of the original cast. Loading is fast throughout. DF's small complaints are that the old flashing hit markers on enemies are gone, making it harder to tell when you're doing damage, and that the longer cutscenes sometimes interrupt the flow.

reviews.headline: 540p–1080p docked DLSS · locked 30fps
reviews.overview: DF found the Switch 2 version holds up well against Xbox Series S, with a sharper but noisier picture and a locked 30 frames per second. Many cuts against PS5 match the Series S, and performance improved noticeably over the earlier demo.

findings.text: The frame rate is [[locked|Locked / capped]] at 30. Cutscene hitches of up to 100ms seen in the demo are much improved, and open areas and towns run better, partly because there are fewer people around.
[[DLSS|DLSS]] rebuilds a 1080p image docked from a [[dynamic|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] 540p to 1080p. The result is crisper than [[Series S|Series S]] but shows noisy artifacts.

Against PS5, [[textures|Texture resolution]] and [[shadow draw distance|Shadow draw distance]] drop to Series S level, plant density in the Grasslands is lower, and [[pop-in|Pop-in]] is more visible. People in the distance freeze in place beyond a set range. Character models look better than on Series S.
[[Volumetric fog|Volumetric lighting / fog]] runs at a low setting with visible [[dithering|Dithering]], and water uses a simpler mesh. All object physics and every cutscene are kept.

reviews.headline: 540p · UE5 · painterly look
reviews.overview: Yoshi and the Mysterious Book renders at a very low resolution for a Switch 2 game, but DF argues that it works. The soft, painterly art style hides the low pixel count, so the game looks charming rather than blurry.

findings.text: The game renders at just 540p when docked and 360p in handheld, far below most Switch 2 games. DF's view is that this is a deliberate fit with the art style rather than a sign the game is struggling, and the [[image quality|Image quality (IQ)]] holds up because nothing in the look depends on crisp edges.

The watercolor, cel-shaded appearance comes from [[post-processing|Post-processing]] effects in Unreal Engine 5. Those filters soften the whole image, which is a big part of why the low resolution doesn't stand out.

This is one of the first Nintendo-published games built on [[Unreal Engine 5|Unreal Engine 5 (UE5)]], so DF also looked at it as an example of how other developers might use the engine on Switch 2. The coverage of DF's findings didn't report a frame rate.

reviews.headline: 720p on PS5 · PS5 Pro shines
reviews.overview: DF calls 007 First Light a technical standout, but the gap between the two PlayStation consoles is unusually large. The standard PS5 runs at a low resolution with a messy upscaler, while the PS5 Pro is where the game truly shines.

findings.text: The standard PS5 offers a choice between 60fps at a low resolution and 30fps at a higher one. The PS5 Pro has only one mode: it takes the base PS5's Quality settings and runs them at 60fps, so you get the better visuals without giving up smoothness.

On the standard PS5, Performance mode renders at just 720p and Quality mode at 1080p, both upscaled with [[FSR]] 3.1. DF found that the upscaler causes noticeable flicker even when the camera is still, and chunky, blocky [[reconstruction artifacts|Disocclusion artifacts]] when moving, especially on [[foliage|Alpha-tested foliage]] as the camera pans. The PS5 Pro uses the updated [[PSSR]] 2, which DF says gives a much cleaner and sharper image.

This is one of the clearest examples so far of what the [[PS5 Pro]] adds. The extra GPU power runs the Quality settings at double the frame rate, and the AI upscaler fixes the image problems the base console can't.

reviews.game: Indiana Jones and the Great Circle
reviews.headline: 540p–1080p docked DLSS · 30fps · ray-traced GI kept
reviews.overview: DF found a solid port that keeps the game's ray-traced lighting, matching or slightly beating Xbox Series S, with a higher resolution too. It runs at 30 frames per second, with cuts to shadows, draw distance and object detail.

findings.text: [[Ray-traced global illumination|RTGI]] is intact and matches, sometimes slightly beats, the [[Series S|Series S]] version. [[Screen-space reflections|Screen-space reflections (SSR)]] and [[contact shadows|Contact shadows]] are kept too.

[[DLSS|DLSS]] reconstructs from a [[dynamic|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] 540p to 1080p docked and 360p to 720p handheld, an overall higher resolution than Series S. Edges show more [[aliasing|Aliasing / jaggies]] than other versions.
The game targets 30 frames per second. Cutscenes drop frames, and heavy combat in the Vatican with many enemies can fall to the mid-20s.

Shadows and object quality are reduced, more so handheld. [[Draw distance|Draw distance]] is shorter, so geometry [[pops in|Pop-in]] more aggressively. [[Textures|Texture resolution]] match Series S without its high-quality texture pack.

reviews.headline: 1440p→4K · 60fps · PSSR on Pro
reviews.overview: DF's verdict on Housemarque's Saros is broadly positive on both consoles, but the PS5 Pro is where it truly excels. The game is built around a smooth 60fps, and the Pro's AI upscaler handles the screen-filling particle effects far better than the standard PS5 can.

findings.text: There is a single 60fps mode, and DF says the frame rate barely ever flinches on PS5 Pro, with slight dips only in the densest sequences. The standard PS5 performs well but a little below the Pro. Real-time cutscenes can drop to 30fps and pre-rendered videos play at 24fps, which creates a small mismatch with the smooth gameplay.

On PS5 Pro, the game renders at around 1440p and uses [[PSSR]] to reconstruct a 4K image. On the standard PS5 it renders at around 1224p and uses AMD's [[FSR]] instead. The base PS5 image is softer and [[flickers|Temporal stability]] more, especially during fast movement.

Saros fills the screen with bullet-hell [[particle effects|Particles]], which are notoriously hard for [[temporal upscalers|Temporal upscaling / reconstruction]] to keep stable. DF says PSSR handles them well on the Pro, keeping them sharp and coherent. On the standard PS5, FSR struggles with them, and particles are the weakest part of the image.

The game is built on [[Unreal Engine 5|Unreal Engine 5 (UE5)]] with Housemarque's own additions, but it skips the engine's heavier features like [[Lumen]] and [[Nanite]] to protect the 60fps target. As a result, [[shadows|Shadow maps]] and [[screen-space reflections|Screen-space reflections (SSR)]] are unremarkable.

reviews.headline: 864p→4K on Pro · up to 120fps
reviews.overview: DF says Pragmata is fine on a standard PS5, but the PS5 Pro is the best way to play. The Pro's new upscaler gives what DF calls a colossal boost in image quality, while the base console's older upscaler leaves the picture looking rough.

findings.text: On the standard PS5, Frame Rate mode is almost locked at 60fps. Resolution mode turns ray tracing back on and loses some frames, which [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] can help smooth out. On PS5 Pro, Frame Rate mode runs at up to 120fps. It isn't consistent, but it stays inside the VRR range, so it still feels smooth on a compatible TV.

The standard PS5 renders at 1080p and uses the old [[FSR 1|FSR]], a [[spatial upscaler|Spatial upscaling]] that works from a single frame, which DF says leads to poor image quality overall. The PS5 Pro uses the updated [[PSSR]] 2 to turn an 864p image into 4K, and the difference is dramatic. Its Frame Rate mode lowers the output to 1440p to reach higher frame rates.

Ray-traced [[screen-space reflections|Screen-space reflections (SSR)]] are switched off in the base PS5's Frame Rate mode. On PS5 Pro, the remaining weak spot is that [[ray-traced reflections|RT reflections]] look low-resolution, because they are calculated from the lower internal resolution before upscaling.

reviews.headline: 540p→1080p DLSS docked · unlocked 30–50fps
reviews.overview: DF called the Switch 2 version a slightly mixed bag. DLSS produces a surprisingly competitive picture, but the frame rate is unlocked with no option to cap it, so it swings between about 30 and 50.

findings.text: Capcom left the frame rate [[unlocked|Unlocked]]. It sits around 30 to 40 frames per second in busy areas and about 50 indoors, and there is no option to [[lock|Locked / capped]] it, so the changes in smoothness are jarring.
Docked upscales a 540p image to 1080p with [[DLSS|DLSS]], which DF called arguably competitive with PS5 for clarity. Handheld starts from just 360p but holds up better than you would expect.
Compared with PS5, lighting is simpler, shadows are worse and textures are simplified. The gap shows most in cutscenes.
Hair lacks the fine [[strand detail|Hair strands / hair cards]] seen on other platforms. DF considers [[Series S|Series S]] a fair match for Switch 2 here, and Switch 2 often looks better.

reviews.headline: 1080p/60 on PS5 · CPU drops on Pro
reviews.overview: DF found Crimson Desert's console versions a mixed bag. The PS5 Pro is the best way to play, but even there CPU-heavy scenes can halve the frame rate, and DF says Pearl Abyss has not made the effort to optimize for 60fps on the standard PS5 at all.

findings.text: On a standard PS5, Performance mode targets 60 frames per second but drops noticeably, Balanced mode mostly holds 40 but needs a [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] display, and Quality mode is locked at 30. On PS5 Pro, the main problem is the processor: in towns, cities and heavy combat the game becomes [[CPU-limited|CPU-bound / CPU-limited]], and the frame rate can be cut in half. With v-sync off and the 120Hz option on, Performance mode can reach around 105fps, but the CPU dips feel even more jarring. DF says it is impossible to ignore the drops in any Pro mode.

Performance mode on the standard PS5 renders at a blurry 1080p. A recent update added a 4K output option that improves the image at the cost of more frame rate. The PS5 Pro uses [[PSSR]] 2, and its Performance mode looks roughly like the standard PS5's Quality mode. The Pro's 30fps Quality mode offers diminishing returns, so DF finds it hard to recommend.

Every mode shows [[shimmering|Shimmering / specular aliasing]] on reflective surfaces like water, and shadowing indoors is visibly broken in places. Quality mode's biggest visual upgrade on the standard PS5 is in character models.

reviews.game: Super Mario Bros. Wonder – Switch 2 Edition
reviews.headline: Native 4K · locked 60fps
reviews.overview: DF ranks this among the best Switch 2 upgrades, on the same level as Splatoon 3's free update. It runs at a native 4K with a perfectly stable 60 frames per second, and the only thing DF wished for was a 120fps option.

findings.text: The game is [[locked|Locked / capped]] at 60 frames per second and DF found it completely stable. The small drops on the world map in the original Switch version are gone.

Docked, the game renders at a [[native|Native resolution]] 4K, meaning every pixel is drawn for real with no upscaling. Handheld renders a native 1080p to match the screen. A few interface elements still use 1080p artwork, so they look slightly softer than the rest of the image on a 4K TV.

DF's only real criticism is the lack of a [[120fps mode|120Hz mode]] at a lower resolution, like the one Metroid Prime 4 offers. A 2D platformer with simple visuals seems like an ideal candidate for one.
This is a paid [[Switch 2 Edition|Next-gen / Pro patch]] that also adds new content, rather than a free patch.

reviews.headline: Unpatched games run smoother · handheld boost
reviews.overview: Even without any update from the developer, many original Switch games run better on Switch 2, because the console's faster hardware lets games with unlocked or dynamic settings stretch further. In March 2026, system update 22.0.0 went further with a handheld boost mode, which DF described as an automatic remaster for much of the Switch library.

findings.title: At launch: unpatched games
findings.text: Switch 2's [[backwards compatibility|Backwards compatibility]] runs original Switch games on much faster hardware. In DF's tests, The Witcher 3 holds a stable 30 frames per second instead of dropping to around 20 in demanding scenes, and its [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] sits noticeably higher because the GPU has room to spare. Batman: Arkham Knight goes from drops as low as 15fps to a stable 30. Without a patch, though, games keep their original low-resolution textures and settings.

findings.title: 2026: handheld boost mode
findings.text: System update 22.0.0 lets original Switch games use their docked graphics settings in [[handheld mode|Docked / handheld mode]]. Games that rendered 720p in handheld, like Mario Kart 8 Deluxe and Luigi's Mansion, can now reach a [[native|Native resolution]] 1080p on the Switch 2 screen. Games with very low resolutions and no [[TAA|TAA (temporal AA)]], like Persona 5 Royal and Yoshi's Crafted World, get much sharper edges and more readable detail.

findings.title: The trade-off
findings.text: Doom, Doom Eternal and Wolfenstein gain higher resolutions and keep graphics options that used to be docked-only. Resident Evil 5's unlocked frame rate rises from around 20 to 30fps to about 50fps. The cost is battery life: boost mode draws more [[power|TDP / power draw]], and Resident Evil 5 used roughly 25% more battery. Results vary from game to game.

reviews.headline: ~720p docked → DLSS · 60fps target (Village dips to 40s)
reviews.overview: DF tested both games together. Resident Evil 7 is the better port, holding 60 frames per second with better image quality than PS4. Village looks fine but drops into the 40s outdoors.

findings.text: Resident Evil 7 targets 60 frames per second without major dips. Village also targets 60 and holds it indoors, but outdoor areas like the reservoir fall into the 40s.

Docked renders around 720p and is upscaled to 1080p, likely with [[DLSS|DLSS]], giving cleaner image quality than PS4. Handheld drops to about 432p. Village's image beats [[Series S|Series S]], but its frame rate doesn't.

[[Screen-space reflections|Screen-space reflections (SSR)]] suffer from the low resolution. In Village, the [[volumetric lighting|Volumetric lighting / fog]] behaves differently and creates thick fog that hides distant detail, and falling snow is barely visible.
Blacks look [[raised|Raised / crushed blacks]] compared with other versions because of how Switch 2 handles gamma.

reviews.headline: 540p docked / 360p handheld → DLSS · unlocked 40–60fps
reviews.overview: DF praised Capcom for this port. DLSS turns a 540p image into one that looks better than Xbox Series S at 720p, but the unlocked frame rate mostly sits in the 40s and 50s.

findings.text: The game renders at just 540p docked and 360p handheld. DF believes it uses the full [[DLSS|DLSS]] model, and the docked result looks better than the [[Series S|Series S]] version at 720p. The interface is drawn at a sharp 1080p.
The frame rate is [[unlocked|Unlocked]] and aims for 60, but mostly runs in the 40s and 50s docked, with the worst dips to 30. DF hopes a patch improves consistency.
Geometry and [[textures|Texture resolution]] are reduced and character hair is handled differently from PS5, but DF said the cuts don't meaningfully affect the experience.
Loading is very quick, and reloading a save is fast too.

reviews.headline: 60fps with RT on Pro · near-4K
reviews.overview: DF says Resident Evil Requiem is excellent on every system but brilliant on PS5 Pro, which is head and shoulders ahead of every other console. They also call it one of the best-looking games released, thanks to its character models and texture detail.

findings.text: The standard PS5 runs at 60fps with what DF calls exceptional performance. On PS5 Pro, the 60fps mode is almost flawless. There is also a 120fps mode that drops ray tracing and the extra upscaling, but with [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] it is a strong alternative for players who want maximum smoothness.

In the PS5 Pro's 60fps mode, the upscaled image looks close to [[native|Native resolution]] 4K even under close inspection. The 120fps mode loses that upscaling, so its image matches the standard PS5.

The PS5 Pro adds [[ray tracing|Ray tracing (RT)]] in its 60fps mode, and the only flaw DF noted was a little noise in the [[reflections|RT reflections]], which is a typical [[denoising|Denoising / denoiser]] limitation. A later patch disabled ray tracing in the Raccoon City section on Pro, which some players criticized as a downgrade.

Character models and [[textures|Texture resolution]] are exceptionally detailed, close enough to see individual threads in clothing, which is a big part of why DF rates it among the best-looking games available.
DF uses this as one of the clearest showcases yet for the [[PS5 Pro]]: the extra power and upscaling turn an already excellent version into the best console version by a wide margin.

reviews.headline: 60fps · smeary upscaling
reviews.overview: The move to 60 frames per second makes Xenoblade Chronicles X feel far more responsive, but DF called this probably the weakest Switch 2 Edition yet because of how it upscales the image. Still screenshots look sharp, while moving scenes smear and warp. DF expects it to be fixed in an update.

findings.text: The game runs at 60 frames per second both docked and handheld, which DF sees as a meaningful upgrade in how responsive it feels to play.

The game renders below 1080p and then uses an unusual upscaler to fill in detail. DF suspects it is a lightweight machine-learning or post-process method rather than the full [[DLSS]] the Switch 2 supports. The game's files point to [[SMAA|FXAA / SMAA]], but the result doesn't look like normal SMAA either. In motion, surfaces [[smear|Ghosting / trails]] with what DF describes as an oil-painting look, and thin objects like cables and power lines look bent instead of straight. The problems are hard to see in still frames and obvious when moving, a classic [[temporal stability|Temporal stability]] issue, and they remain visible even on the handheld screen.

reviews.headline: 1440p/30 · 1080p/60 · thin Pro upgrade
reviews.overview: DF says Avowed's arrival on PS5 is a solid port of an excellent game, but its PS5 Pro features are thin on the ground. The standard PS5 actually edges ahead of Xbox in the unlocked modes, while the Pro adds almost nothing.

findings.text: There are three modes targeting 30, 40 and 60 frames per second, matching the Xbox Series X. With the frame rate unlocked on a [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] display, Performance mode averages in the mid-60s and Balanced mode in the mid-to-high 40s. DF found the PS5 unexpectedly ahead of Xbox here, thanks to better VRR handling.

Internal resolution tops out at 1440p in Quality mode and 1080p in Performance mode. The Xbox Series X hits its 1440p target more often, so it looks slightly sharper, though DF calls the difference subtle.
The [[PS5 Pro]] uses essentially the same settings and resolution as the Xbox Series X, so DF describes its enhancements as about as basic as they can get.

reviews.headline: 792–1296p · 60fps · pop-in
reviews.overview: DF liked Nioh 3's gameplay and art style but was unimpressed by Team Ninja's Katana Engine. Open areas are full of visual bugs and pop-in, and the 30fps mode is hard to recommend, so the 60fps mode is the way to play on either console.

findings.text: Both consoles mostly hold 60 frames per second in Performance mode, with brief drops in chaotic fights that [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] helps smooth out. The 30fps Resolution mode halves the frame rate, adds [[input lag|Input latency / input lag]] and has uneven [[frame pacing|Frame pacing]], so it feels less smooth than expected.

On PS5 Pro, resolution [[changes dynamically|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] between about 792p and 1296p in Performance mode and reaches 1440p in Resolution mode, upscaled with [[PSSR]]. The standard PS5 runs 720p to 1152p in Performance mode and a fixed 1152p in Resolution mode, upscaled with [[FSR]]. The Pro image is more stable, with less flicker on hair, foliage and armor. The trade-offs are slightly softer still images, less stable reflections and noticeable [[shimmering|Shimmering / specular aliasing]] when the resolution changes.
Open fields suffer from visual bugs and [[pop-in|Pop-in]] of geometry and shadows, even in the 30fps mode. It doesn't ruin the experience, but it is constant while exploring.

The Pro has cleaner [[screen-space reflections|Screen-space reflections (SSR)]] and a slightly longer [[shadow draw distance|Shadow draw distance]]. Unlike Rise of the Ronin, there are no ray-traced reflections.

reviews.headline: 1080p docked · stable 30fps
reviews.overview: DF called this a technical triumph for Switch 2. It is a hybrid of the PS4 and PS5 versions: PS5-style lighting and many PS5 textures, with PS4-level shadows and pop-in, at a stable 30 frames per second.

findings.text: The lighting follows the PS5 Intergrade release, which reworked the original PS4 game's lighting and fog. Shadows are closer to the PS4 version.

Many environment [[textures|Texture resolution]] are close to PS5 quality, which fixes some famously blurry surfaces from the PS4 original, such as doors in the Sector 7 slums. A few textures still lean toward PS4, and character [[pop-in|Pop-in]] is also PS4-like.
Performance is solid in both modes at a stable 30 frames per second. Handheld shows very minor dips when turning the camera in a few areas, such as Aerith's house.
DF expects Final Fantasy VII Rebirth to be the real test for Switch 2, since it is a much larger open game.

reviews.headline: ~648p→DLSS docked / ~400p handheld · 30fps
reviews.overview: DF called it an impossible port that impresses. It comes very close to the Xbox Series S version in looks and mostly holds 30 frames per second, but frame pacing is poor.

findings.text: The game mostly holds its 30 frames per second target, with occasional dips in demanding places and in cutscenes. The bigger issue is [[frame pacing|Frame pacing]]: frames aren't delivered evenly, so motion looks less smooth than the number suggests.

Docked renders around 648p before [[DLSS|DLSS]] upscales it, and DF said the result looks much better than that figure implies. Handheld drops as low as 400p but still looks respectable on the smaller screen, and DF found it the more reliable way to play.
Handheld mode drops [[screen-space reflections|Screen-space reflections (SSR)]], so water loses most of its reflections and looks flat. Shadows are also weaker than on other consoles.
Foliage is thinned out in the middle distance and [[textures|Texture resolution]] are lower resolution. The Switch 2 version takes about half the storage of the Series S one.

reviews.headline: 1440p/60 or 1080p/120 · superb HDR
reviews.overview: DF calls Metroid Prime 4: Beyond truly beautiful, with the best image quality they had seen from a Nintendo game on Switch 2 at the time. It offers a choice between a sharper 60fps mode and a 120fps mode, and its HDR is among the best DF has seen on any platform in years.

findings.text: There are two [[modes|Performance / Quality mode]]. The 120 frames per second mode is [[locked|Locked / capped]] and holds with near-total consistency, with only a rare tiny dip while riding through the open world. The 60fps Quality mode is just as smooth, so either choice plays well.

Quality mode renders at 1440p docked and 1080p handheld, and on a TV the image reads close to 4K. The visor frame around the screen is drawn separately from the main view, which helps it look crisp. Performance mode drops to 1080p docked and 720p handheld to reach 120fps, and still looks sharp, noticeably cleaner than Metroid Prime Remastered on the original Switch.

[[HDR|HDR (high dynamic range)]] is the standout feature. DF describes it as one of the finest HDR presentations in years, alongside the very best on any platform. It looks best on a TV, because the Switch 2's built-in screen can't get as bright. To use the 120fps mode on a TV, you need one that supports [[120Hz|120Hz mode]].

Small details like reflections on Samus's visor, rain droplets and light breaking through cracks add a lot to the atmosphere. Loading is quick as well, and doors open much faster than in earlier Prime games, which used them to hide loading.

reviews.headline: 1080p · 60fps · RTXGI
reviews.overview: DF calls Kirby Air Riders a very polished experience that nails the fundamentals. It runs on a brand-new engine with a distinctive look and solid performance, but its HDR is a real weak point.

findings.text: Docked play is close to a stable 60 frames per second, with only the occasional dropped frame. City Trial, where many racers share one large open map, is the heaviest mode and runs at roughly 40 to 50fps with more frequent drops. Three- and four-player split-screen also aims for 60 but often lands just under it.

There is no [[120fps option|120Hz mode]], which DF would have liked for a racing game. The [[HDR|HDR (high dynamic range)]] is very poor: only particle effects get brighter, while everything else looks dim and washed out, so most players will be better off with HDR turned off.

Resolution [[changes dynamically|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]]. Docked, it is mostly 1080p and reaches 1440p in some scenes, and handheld usually sits around 900p within a range of 720p to 1080p.

The game uses Nvidia's RTXGI to add [[global illumination|Global illumination (GI)]] to moving objects, so karts and characters pick up bounced light from their surroundings. The environments rely on simpler [[baked lightmaps|Baked lighting / lightmaps]] rather than full ray tracing, which DF says is a sensible choice that keeps performance high.
The game is built on a new [[engine|Game engine]] called SOL-AVES. DF thinks this is only the beginning, and expects later games on the same engine to look even more impressive.

reviews.headline: 1440p · 60fps · DLSS · lots of pop-in
reviews.overview: DF describes Pokémon Legends: Z-A as rough around the edges and garish even on Switch 2. The upside is that the Switch 2 version is night and day compared with the original Switch, with a much sharper image and a locked 60 frames per second.

findings.text: On Switch 2 the game is [[locked|Locked / capped]] at 60 frames per second with very rare drops. The original Switch version targets 30fps and often falls into the 20s when you pan the camera, so the difference in smoothness is huge.
Switch 2 targets 1440p docked and 1080p handheld, using Nvidia's [[DLSS]] to upscale to those resolutions. This is the main reason the image looks so much cleaner than on the original Switch.

[[Pop-in]] is heavy on both systems. Buildings and details appear late, and pedestrians appear or vanish as you walk toward them because of aggressive [[level-of-detail|Level of detail (LOD)]] settings. [[Textures|Texture resolution]] are sharper on Switch 2, but repeated flat textures on building windows and balconies look pixelated up close, which DF calls a major weakness for a game set in a city.

Because the game is [[cross-gen|Next-gen / current-gen / cross-gen]], built for both Switch and Switch 2, DF's [[side-by-side|Side-by-side / head-to-head]] comparison shows one of the biggest gaps between the two consoles in any game so far.

reviews.headline: 720–900p · ~60fps · huge crowds
reviews.overview: DF calls Age of Imprisonment pretty decent overall. It puts huge crowds of enemies and heavy effects on screen while keeping the frame rate mostly stable, and its resolution targets are sensible for such a busy game.

findings.text: The game aims for 60 frames per second and mostly gets there. You will notice drops, but it rarely falls below 50fps. Local split-screen co-op runs at 30fps, while co-op across two consoles or through GameShare keeps 60.

Resolution [[changes dynamically|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] to protect the frame rate. Docked, it moves between 720p and 900p, and handheld between 468p and 648p. Those are low numbers, but DF thinks they are a fair trade for the amount of action on screen.
Many attacks produce effects that [[cast light onto the terrain|Emissive lighting]] around them, which makes the big combat moments look more dramatic.
The headline feature is scale: [[dozens of enemies|Object / crowd density]] can be on screen at once at 60fps, and they are much more detailed than in the previous game, Age of Calamity.
Combat stacks many [[particle effects|Particles]] and [[transparent effects|Alpha effects / transparencies]] on top of each other, and the game handles them without falling apart.

reviews.headline: 30 / 60 / 120fps · 80–100 on Pro
reviews.overview: DF found Ninja Gaiden 4 delivers stable performance and smooth, engaging combat. It isn't the series' graphical peak, but the 60fps mode is the best balance, and the PS5 Pro runs it noticeably faster.

findings.text: The standard PS5 offers three modes. The 30fps mode has poor [[frame pacing|Frame pacing]] and looks worse than you'd expect. The 60fps mode is the best balance, with noticeable drops only in complex battles. The 120fps mode is very smooth but cuts visual quality. On PS5 Pro with [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] and the frame rate unlocked, the game runs at roughly 80 to 100fps, so the 120fps mode becomes optional.
DF praised the soundtrack and the feel of the combat, and summed it up as a technically solid release rather than a showcase.

reviews.headline: Xbox ahead · PS5 Pro struggles at launch
reviews.overview: DF found the Xbox versions of The Outer Worlds 2 clearly better at launch, with three solid modes, while the experience on PS5 consoles needs improvement in a number of areas. The PS5 Pro in particular may be the worst place to play it at launch.

findings.text: The PS5 Pro shows clear frame-rate drops whatever mode you choose, and more [[stutter|Stutter / hitch]] than the Xbox Series X. The standard PS5 trails the Xbox slightly in both resolution and performance.
At launch, the Pro used [[PSSR]], and its noisy reconstruction was a big part of the problem. A later patch temporarily replaced it with Unreal's [[TSR|TAAU / TSR]], the same upscaler the Xbox uses.
With the more basic lighting and ray tracing combination on the Pro, objects often look noisy and poorly defined. The Xbox Series X lighting doesn't degrade the image the same way.

reviews.game: Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2
reviews.headline: 4K docked · near-flawless 60fps
reviews.overview: DF calls this collection a clean upgrade overall, and a lovely, if pricey, treat for fans. The headline improvements are 4K on Switch 2 and much better textures.

findings.text: Performance was already good, with very few drops on the original Switch, and there are even fewer on Switch 2.
Docked on Switch 2, the games run at a 4K [[output resolution|Output resolution]], up from 1080p on the original Switch.

Upgraded [[textures|Texture resolution]] are the biggest improvement. Grass, walls and planet surfaces are far more detailed, to the point that you can see the stitching on Mario's overalls. Galaxy 2 also gets sharper character [[models|Polygons / triangles]].
Some skies show [[color banding|Color banding]], where a smooth gradient breaks into visible steps.
Pre-rendered cutscenes use low-bitrate video, so they look soft next to the sharp gameplay, a common issue in [[remasters|Remaster / remake]].

reviews.headline: Native 4K on Pro · solid 60fps
reviews.overview: DF found Dying Light: The Beast in good shape on all three major consoles, with nearly identical settings and a mostly solid 60 frames per second. The PS5 Pro mainly adds resolution, reaching a native 4K in Quality mode.

findings.text: All three consoles mostly hold 60 frames per second with occasional slight drops as the camera moves. With the frame rate unlocked, they average around 65fps and can pass 85 indoors.

In Quality mode, the standard PS5 renders at about 1728p and the PS5 Pro at a [[native|Native resolution]] 4K. In the [[dynamic|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] Performance mode, the standard PS5 targets 1080p and never goes below 972p, while the Pro ranges from 1260p to 1512p. DF's figures were notably better than an earlier comparison from another channel, mainly because of how dynamic resolution was counted.
Quality mode improves shadows, [[draw distance|Draw distance]] and vegetation, otherwise the settings are practically identical across consoles.

reviews.headline: 4 modes · RTGI · 60fps RT on Pro
reviews.overview: DF found Ghost of Yōtei beautiful, smooth and technically assured on both consoles. Sucker Punch offers a wide spread of modes, including ray-traced global illumination, and a patch two months after launch made the PS5 Pro version dramatically smoother.

findings.text: Quality mode is locked at 30 frames per second and Performance mode at 60. Before the day-one patch, frame rates could dip to around 50, but the patch fixed that. Patch 1.1, released in late November 2025, added [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] support, a new 40fps [[Balanced mode]], and an option to uncap the frame rate. With it, the PS5 Pro's ray-tracing mode jumps from 60fps to roughly 70 to 90fps, which DF called incredible, and the non-ray-traced modes gain about a third more performance. On a standard PS5 with a 120Hz VRR display, the uncapped Balanced mode can reach 60fps.

Quality mode renders at 4K on both consoles. Performance mode runs at 1080p on PS5 and 1440p on PS5 Pro, so the Pro gives a noticeably sharper 60fps image. The Pro-only 60fps ray-tracing mode renders at 1080p and uses [[PSSR]] to reconstruct a higher-resolution image.

The ray-tracing modes add [[ray-traced global illumination|RTGI]], which DF says noticeably improves how light bounces around the world. The 60fps ray-tracing mode on PS5 Pro has some compromises, with visible [[noise|Denoising / denoiser]] on fabrics and fine detail, since fewer rays can be traced in each frame.

[[HDR|HDR (high dynamic range)]] is a highlight. DF praised it as one of the strongest parts of the presentation, alongside the detail on close-up objects and the improved animation since Ghost of Tsushima.

DF says the game is responsibly optimized for the standard PS5, with stable performance and impressive lighting and weather. The [[PS5 Pro]] mainly adds sharper Performance mode, 60fps ray tracing and, after the patch, much higher frame rates.

findings.title: QSSR on standard PS5 (October 2026)
findings.text: DF also tested [[QSSR]] in Ghost of Yōtei's performance mode on the standard PS5. The improvement is less dramatic because the game's image was already clean, and the performance cost was barely noticeable.

reviews.headline: Strong on PS5 · broken PSSR on Pro (fixed 2026)
reviews.overview: DF found Silent Hill f impressive on a standard PS5 but problematic on PS5 Pro at launch, where a forced and poorly tuned PSSR caused shimmering and odd lighting. A March 2026 update to the upgraded PSSR fixed those problems and turned the Pro version into a showcase.

findings.text: The PS5 Pro has a single Enhanced mode that blends the standard PS5's Performance and Quality modes and runs at a mostly smooth 60 frames per second.

The internal resolutions are low. Other outlets measured Performance mode on the standard PS5 at 360p to 720p, upscaled to 1800p, while Quality mode renders around 720p and upscales to 4K at 30fps. At launch, the Pro forced [[PSSR]] on with no way to turn it off, and DF found near-constant [[shimmering|Shimmering / specular aliasing]] over grass, which led some players to prefer the standard PS5.

On the Pro at launch, objects in the middle distance were lit oddly and the [[ray-traced global illumination|RTGI]] visibly pulsed. After the March 2026 PSSR upgrade, DF says the pulsing is gone, foliage renders consistently, and textures and characters look sharper without the grainy, film-like noise. They called it a transformation from a demonstration of PSSR's failures into a showcase.

reviews.headline: Gets slower the longer you play
reviews.overview: DF confirmed that Borderlands 4 has a serious problem on every console: performance gets worse the longer you play. Restarting the game temporarily fixes it, which DF calls effective but unacceptable as something players should have to do.

findings.text: Performance mode can start at 60 frames per second, but after about 30 minutes the frame rate begins to slide, and within an hour it falls into the 40s, even in a simple room. One new area dipped into the 30s. This happens on the PS5 Pro and Xbox Series X too, so more powerful hardware doesn't solve it. Quitting and relaunching the game resets performance for a while, but even then the drops eventually return.

A problem like this, where performance degrades over time rather than in specific scenes, usually points to a software bug, such as memory not being cleaned up properly, rather than the console simply being too slow. Until a patch arrives, the more stable 30fps Quality mode is the safer choice.

reviews.headline: DLSS to 1440p docked · 30fps · ray tracing
reviews.overview: DF called this the most impressive Switch 2 port to date at the time. It keeps the game's ray-traced lighting, runs at a fairly consistent 30 frames per second, and compares better with Xbox Series S than DF expected.

findings.text: The game keeps its [[ray tracing|Ray tracing (RT)]], which DF highlighted because Outlaws was built around ray-traced lighting and has no simpler fallback. [[Volumetric fog and lighting|Volumetric lighting / fog]] are reduced slightly compared with other consoles.
[[DLSS|DLSS]] lets the docked image reach a 1440p output, and image quality held up against the [[Series S|Series S]] version better than DF had expected.
Gameplay holds a fairly consistent 30 frames per second. The only drops DF noted were a few lost frames in cutscenes and pre-rendered videos.
Switch 2 is weaker than Series S in raw power, but DF said its more modern graphics features, especially DLSS, let this game punch above its weight.

reviews.headline: 60fps works · 989–1432p on PS5
reviews.overview: Hellblade II arrived on PS5 in its Enhanced edition with a new 60fps mode, and DF's verdict is simple: 60fps works, and it works well. The visual gap from the 30fps mode is small outside close-up comparisons.

findings.text: The 60fps Performance mode holds up well with only minor drops, and the PS5 Pro had the fewest, just one in DF's testing.

On a standard PS5, Quality mode renders around 1432p and Performance around 989p, a little lower than Xbox Series X, with Unreal's [[TSR|TAAU / TSR]] reconstructing to 4K and 1440p. On PS5 Pro, Quality averages about 1696p and Performance about 1166p, both reconstructed to 4K. The Pro lets you choose between [[PSSR]] and TSR. DF slightly prefers TSR because PSSR shows noise on bright reflections, though PSSR holds up better in motion.
Ninja Theory moved the game to a newer version of [[Unreal Engine 5|Unreal Engine 5 (UE5)]] to support PSSR on the Pro, keeping the photorealistic [[Lumen]] lighting the original was praised for.

reviews.headline: 540p–864p perf / 810p balanced / 1188p quality → 1800p
reviews.overview: DF found plenty of graphics options but few good ones. Resolutions are very low, frame pacing is uneven in every mode, and DF recommends the 60fps performance mode as the least bad choice.

findings.text: Every mode outputs 1800p, but the [[internal resolution|Internal / base resolution]] is far lower: 864p dropping to 540p in performance mode, 810p in balanced and 1188p in quality. The visual differences between modes are mainly [[ambient occlusion|Ambient occlusion (AO)]] and foliage [[draw distance|Draw distance]].

Performance mode is the one DF recommends. Quality mode's 30fps has uneven [[frame pacing|Frame pacing]] and heavy [[motion blur|Motion blur (camera)]]. The [[balanced|Balanced mode]] 40fps mode only makes sense on a 120Hz screen; on 60Hz it runs unlocked and [[tears|Screen tearing]] constantly. Frequent autosaves also cause dips.
On [[PS5 Pro|PS5 Pro]] the picture looks the same, with a slightly higher dynamic resolution and steadier frame rate. DF suggests leaving the unlocked frame rate option off on every console.

reviews.game: Kirby and the Forgotten Land – Switch 2 Edition
reviews.headline: 1440p · locked 60fps (was 30)
reviews.overview: DF sees this as a solid upgrade over the original Switch release, mainly because the game now runs at a locked 60 frames per second instead of 30. The visual overhaul is smaller than in the Zelda Switch 2 Editions, but the paid upgrade also adds the new Star-Crossed World content.

findings.text: The biggest change is smoothness. The original Switch version ran at 30 frames per second, and the Switch 2 Edition is [[locked|Locked / capped]] at 60 in both docked and handheld play.

Docked, the game targets 1440p and uses [[dynamic resolution scaling|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] to drop lower in more complex stages. Handheld targets 1080p, matching the screen. Edges are smoothed with [[SMAA|FXAA / SMAA]], which mostly works but leaves some rough spots on fine detail.

DF considers this a meaningful [[Switch 2 Edition|Next-gen / Pro patch]], though a smaller visual leap than Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom got. The paid upgrade also includes Star-Crossed World, a new chunk of content built for Switch 2.

reviews.game: Zelda: Breath of the Wild & Tears of the Kingdom – Switch 2 Editions
reviews.headline: 1440p · stable 60fps · FSR 1
reviews.overview: DF calls these upgrades transformative. Both games finally run at a smooth 60 frames per second with a much sharper image and faster loading, although some weaknesses of the original Switch versions remain.

findings.text: Both games now hold a stable 60 frames per second docked and handheld, where the originals often struggled to stay at 30. Tears of the Kingdom has only rare blips, even with its physics-heavy building.

Resolution [[changes dynamically|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]]. Docked, it targets 1440p, up from 900p, but can drop as low as 810p in demanding moments like building with Ultrahand. Handheld ranges from 648p to 1080p. Upscaling still appears to use the older [[FSR 1|FSR]], a [[spatial upscaler|Spatial upscaling]] that works from a single frame, rather than [[DLSS]]. [[Anti-aliasing|Anti-aliasing (AA)]] ranges from weak to almost absent, so edges stay [[jagged|Aliasing / jaggies]]. In Tears, the image also drops to a blurrier 810p for a few frames whenever the camera changes view.
[[Shadows|Shadow maps]] near the camera are higher resolution but flicker, and [[ambient occlusion|Ambient occlusion (AO)]], the soft darkening in corners and creases, is thicker than before.

Higher-resolution [[textures|Texture resolution]] make grass, brickwork and shield designs much sharper, at the cost of a bigger download. [[Texture filtering|Anisotropic filtering (AF)]] is still low, so surfaces at an angle look blurry, and [[draw distance|Draw distance]] is largely unchanged. Load times are much shorter thanks to the Switch 2's faster [[storage|SSD / NVMe]].

reviews.headline: 720p→1080p DLSS docked · 30fps
reviews.overview: DF found the Switch 2 version a big improvement over the heavily cut-back original Switch release, with lighting and detail closer to the PS4 and Xbox One versions.

findings.text: The game renders at a low [[internal resolution|Internal / base resolution]], 720p docked and 540p handheld, and uses [[DLSS|DLSS]] to rebuild a 1080p picture.

Compared with the original Switch version, this one adds [[global illumination|Global illumination (GI)]], better [[ambient occlusion|SSAO / HBAO / GTAO]], more shadow-casting lights and [[screen-space reflections|Screen-space reflections (SSR)]] on water and shiny floors. The overall settings are similar to the Xbox One S version.
Models and textures are a large step up from Switch 1, and some textures are sharper than on last-generation consoles. Foliage is a little patchier than on PS4.
Most of the loading screens that broke up the Switch 1 version are gone, so the castle and the world feel connected again.

reviews.headline: 1080–1200p · 60fps with 30fps bosses
reviews.overview: DF's verdict on Donkey Kong Bananza is somewhat mixed. The voxel-based destruction is genuinely impressive, but frame-rate drops, dated shadows and a soft image hold it back, and DF hopes updates will fix some of it.

findings.text: The game targets 60 frames per second but [[slows down|Stutter / hitch]] during certain animations, such as picking up bananas, and during camera cuts. Some boss fights drop to 30fps and stay there for the entire fight, and photo mode also runs at about 30.
Handheld play runs a little better because the screen supports [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]], which smooths out small drops, though it doesn't remove them entirely.

Docked, the resolution [[changes dynamically|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] between roughly 1080p and 1200p, and some areas look soft. The game uses AMD's older [[FSR 1|FSR]] rather than Nvidia's [[DLSS]], so the environment shows noticeable [[aliasing|Aliasing / jaggies]]. Handheld image quality is better, at what looks like 1080p.

Lighting looks dated, and DF calls the [[shadow rendering|Shadow maps]] extremely poor and distracting. They compare it unfavorably with Super Mario Odyssey's Switch 2 update, which cleaned up many similar issues.

The [[destruction|Physics / destruction]] is the highlight. You can dig through almost anything to open new routes, and the camera copes well underground. The breaking animation itself is choppy, though, especially in the 30fps boss fights. [[Pop-in]] is also frequent.

reviews.game: Free Switch 2 updates: Mario, Zelda & Splatoon
reviews.headline: 7 games · 60fps locked · up to 4K
reviews.overview: When Switch 2 launched, Nintendo released free updates for several original Switch games. DF tested seven of them and called each one a really nice upgrade, essentially remasters in everything but name, and praised Nintendo for giving them away for free. The two top-down Zelda games improved the most, because their biggest technical flaws are simply gone.

modes.mode: New Super Mario Bros. U Deluxe

findings.title: Zelda: Link's Awakening and Echoes of Wisdom
findings.text: These were the biggest wins. On the original Switch, both games had very uneven frame rates, especially Link's Awakening, which stuttered constantly. On Switch 2 they run at a consistent 60 frames per second at higher resolutions. DF said Link's Awakening is borderline like a free [[remaster|Remaster / remake]], because the main technical flaw of the original is completely gone.

findings.title: Super Mario Odyssey
findings.text: Docked resolution roughly doubles, from a [[dynamic|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] 900p or so to a dynamic 1800p, and handheld now renders a [[native|Native resolution]] 1080p. The frame rate is [[locked|Locked / capped]] at 60 with no drops, so the game looks much sharper while feeling exactly as smooth as it should.

findings.title: Splatoon 3
findings.text: Docked resolution jumps from a dynamic 1080p to a full 4K, and handheld runs at 1080p. The game now holds 60fps everywhere, including the busy city hub, which used to run at 30 on the original Switch.

findings.title: Super Mario 3D World + Bowser's Fury
