findings.text: Bowser's Fury, the open-world add-on that struggled on Switch 1, now runs at a dynamic 1800p with higher-resolution [[shadow maps|Shadow maps]] and a locked 60fps. Handheld play is a huge step up at 1080p and 60fps. DF called the results pretty darn impressive.

findings.title: Captain Toad and New Super Mario Bros. U Deluxe
findings.text: Captain Toad rises from 1080p to 1440p docked and 1080p handheld at a consistent 60fps. New Super Mario Bros. U Deluxe reaches 4K docked and 1080p handheld at 60fps. Both are improvements, but they're less noticeable because the simple art styles already looked clean, and the games already ran well.

findings.title: HDR
findings.text: Switch 2 can also apply [[HDR|HDR (high dynamic range)]] to these games, and DF's video covers how it looks across these updates.

reviews.headline: 1440p→4K · 30 or 60fps · exemplary
reviews.overview: John Linneman calls Death Stranding 2 a technical masterpiece and one of the best-looking games of this console generation. Performance and image quality are exemplary on both the standard PS5 and the PS5 Pro, and the main choice is which mode to use.

findings.text: Performance mode runs at 60 frames per second and Quality mode is locked at 30, and both run very smoothly. Performance mode also supports [[120Hz|120Hz mode]] displays.

Both consoles render at around 1440p in Performance mode and upscale to a 4K output. On the standard PS5, the upscaling causes some [[instability|Temporal stability]] in fine detail. On the PS5 Pro, the same reconstruction looks much cleaner.

Distant terrain is more detailed on the PS5 Pro, a difference DF describes as subtle but meaningful. That's why their recommendation differs by console. On a standard PS5, the 30fps Quality mode gives you the full visual experience, so there is a real trade-off between [[distant detail|Level of detail (LOD)]] and smoothness. On a PS5 Pro, the gap between modes is so small that DF calls Quality mode largely redundant, and Performance mode is the clear choice.

Environments are full of exceptionally fine detail, and weather has a real effect on gameplay. DF singles out the [[water simulation|Water simulation / caustics]] in rivers and lakes as especially impressive.

This is Kojima Productions' second game on Guerrilla's Decima [[engine|Game engine]], and DF says the studio now uses it in an even more refined way than Guerrilla does in the Horizon games, with a more dynamic world and top-quality character animation.

reviews.game: Pokémon Scarlet and Violet – Switch 2 update
reviews.headline: 1080p · ~60fps (was sub-30) · fast loads
reviews.overview: DF singles this out as perhaps the most substantial free Switch 2 upgrade. The original Switch version was infamous for its poor performance, and on Switch 2 it runs at around 60 frames per second with a cleaner image and much faster loading. It still looks rough in places, but it is far more enjoyable to play.

findings.text: The frame rate mostly sits around 60 frames per second, dipping in busy scenes, compared with well below 30 on the original Switch. Distant characters and objects now animate smoothly too, instead of updating at a choppy [[reduced rate|Half-rate animation]].
The game renders at a solid 1080p internally. Many expected Nintendo's [[DLSS]] upscaler to be involved, but DF didn't confirm it.

[[Draw distance]] is largely unchanged from the original, and [[pop-in|Pop-in]] is still a problem. Textures remain blocky and many environments still look bland, so the update fixes how the game runs more than how it looks. Pokémon also still vanish when you leave an area and come back.
Fast travel now takes around 3 to 4 seconds instead of up to 15 on the original Switch, thanks to the faster processor and [[storage|SSD / NVMe]].

reviews.headline: Up to 1080p DLSS · 30fps quality / 40fps performance
reviews.overview: DF called the Switch 2 launch port of Cyberpunk impressive. The main story holds up well and looks clearer than the PS4 version thanks to DLSS, but the Phantom Liberty expansion pushes the console below its target.

findings.text: Quality mode holds its 30 frames per second target through the main story. Performance mode aims for a [[40fps mode|40fps mode]]: it reaches that indoors but falls to around 30 outside and in busy shootouts. DF expects handheld to be the smoothest way to play, because the built-in screen supports [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]].

Every mode uses [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] and [[DLSS|DLSS]] to build the final image, which makes it look clearer than the PS4 version. In fast action DLSS shows some blur and noise, because it has few pixels to work from.

[[Texture quality|Texture resolution]] matches PS5 in most places. The number of pedestrians and cars is much closer to PS4, so Night City feels emptier. Indoor shadows beat PS4, while outdoor sun shadows are slightly worse.

Phantom Liberty never came to PS4 because its Dogtown area was too demanding. It is included here, and it is where the Switch 2 struggles most, dropping to roughly 20 to 25 frames per second in quality mode.

reviews.headline: 1440p · locked 60fps
reviews.overview: DF calls Mario Kart World a tremendous accomplishment. The open-world scale is impressive for a launch game, but what stands out most is Nintendo's art direction.

findings.text: Single player is [[locked|Locked / capped]] at 60 frames per second in everything DF tested, and split-screen and online play showed no performance concerns. Photo mode runs at 30fps.

Docked, the game renders at 1440p with a [[post-processing|Post-processing]] pass applied to the image. In handheld it renders exactly 1080p to match the screen, with no [[anti-aliasing|Anti-aliasing (AA)]]. Both are well up on Mario Kart 8 Deluxe, which ran at 1080p docked and 720p handheld.

[[HDR|HDR (high dynamic range)]] looks decent on a TV, but the Switch 2's LCD screen is a weak point for HDR in handheld. Load times from internal [[storage|SSD / NVMe]] are fast, comparable to many current-generation games.

reviews.headline: No stable 60 anywhere · no Pro mode
reviews.overview: DF was disappointed: Nightreign shows no technical progress over Elden Ring from 2021, which already had performance problems. No console holds a stable 60 frames per second, and the PS5 Pro gets no dedicated enhancements at all.

findings.text: Quality mode renders at native 4K with an unlocked frame rate that bounces irregularly between 30 and 45 on PS5, which DF says makes no practical sense. Performance mode targets 60 but drops frequently. The PS5 Pro does a little better through raw power alone, averaging 40 to 60 in Quality mode, but still isn't stable.

Performance mode lowers [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] to 1440p on PS5 and cuts textures, shadows and vegetation. On PS5 Pro, the dynamic resolution sits closer to 4K, but the same visual cuts remain.
There is no [[PS5 Pro]] Enhanced mode. Any gains come only from the stronger hardware, with no dedicated work from the developer.

reviews.headline: Up to 1800p on Pro · drops below 60
reviews.overview: DF called Doom: The Dark Ages one of the less exciting PS5 Pro updates in recent big releases. Both PlayStation consoles drop below 60 frames per second in busy fights, while the Xbox Series X looks largely locked.

findings.text: Both the standard PS5 and the PS5 Pro dip below their 60fps target during busy sequences. That stands out because the Xbox Series X version looks largely locked, which suggests the PlayStation versions got less attention.
The PS5 Pro reaches up to 1800p but doesn't use [[PSSR]] to upscale the image, so it gains little over the standard PS5. DF hoped later patches would improve the PlayStation versions.
Built on id Tech 8, which requires ray-tracing hardware and uses [[ray-traced global illumination|RTGI]] on every platform.

reviews.headline: 864p–1440p · Lumen · 30 or 60fps
reviews.overview: DF was broadly positive about Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, calling it a strong use of Unreal Engine 5. It uses the engine's headline lighting and geometry features well, with a few rough edges in cutscenes and image quality.

findings.text: The game uses [[Lumen]] for dynamic global illumination, [[Nanite]] for very detailed geometry, and virtual [[shadow maps|Shadow maps]], and DF praised how well they come together. Performance mode uses less accurate indirect lighting to reach 60fps.

Resolution is dynamic. The standard PS5 averages around 1224p in Quality mode and around 864p in Performance mode, essentially the same as Xbox Series X. The PS5 Pro averages about 1440p and 1080p respectively. Upscaling uses Unreal's [[TSR|TAAU / TSR]], which leaves noticeable [[aliasing|Aliasing / jaggies]] in some scenes.
Gameplay runs at 30 or 60 frames per second depending on the mode, but cutscenes are capped at 30fps on every platform. Cutscenes also show compression artifacts and some lip-sync issues.

reviews.game: Indiana Jones and the Great Circle
reviews.headline: 1200–1800p · 60fps · cleanest on Pro
reviews.overview: DF considers the PS5 version a successful port of the Xbox and PC original, with refined lighting and shading. The PS5 Pro has the cleanest image of any console, though its other benefits are limited, and the Xbox Series X edges out the standard PS5 on sharpness.

findings.text: The standard PS5 uses the same 1200p to 1800p [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] range as Xbox Series X, but the Xbox tends to sit higher on average, so it looks a little sharper in dense jungle. The PS5 Pro can reach a native 4K and has the cleanest image of the three, with sharper clothing detail and grass.

All three consoles show small [[hitches|Stutter / hitch]] during autosaves and minor drops on cutscene cuts. In the explosion scene in the Vatican crypts, the standard PS5 falls to around 40fps, the PS5 Pro dips to around 50, and the Series X stays near 60.

The PS5 version got refined lighting and shading work. The main blemish is shadow detail on floors that [[pops in|Pop-in]] at roughly one-metre intervals as you walk, an issue present since the original launch.
The PS5 version adds adaptive trigger support for the DualSense controller.

reviews.headline: 1080p docked · ~30fps · big Wii U upgrade
reviews.overview: DF calls this Switch version of the 2015 Wii U game a genuine improvement across the board. It is sharper and loads faster than the original, though performance is mostly unchanged.

findings.text: [[Dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] tops out at a native 1080p docked, which makes the image noticeably sharper than the Wii U original. Handheld mostly matches the 720p screen.

The game mostly holds a steady 30 frames per second but isn't locked to it, so performance is broadly the same as on Wii U. DF found a 60fps setting hidden in the game's code, which hinted at the later Switch 2 Edition.
Loading is faster from the start, and the separate installation packs the Wii U version needed are gone.
Pre-rendered videos have raised black levels, so they look washed out, which wasn't a problem on Wii U.

reviews.headline: RTGI at 60fps on Pro · huge upgrade
reviews.overview: DF calls Assassin's Creed Shadows one of the largest PS5 Pro upgrades they've seen, describing the difference in lighting as a generational divide. The key is that the Pro can run ray-traced global illumination at 60 frames per second.

findings.text: On the standard PS5, [[ray-traced global illumination|RTGI]] is only available in the 30fps Quality mode. The PS5 Pro adds it to the 60fps Performance mode, along with extra ray-traced specular detail. The result is far more convincing light: areas under tree cover look dim and flat on the standard PS5, while on the Pro light filters through the canopy with strong contrast between sun and shade. Shadows from sliding screen doors also move on the Pro but not on the standard PS5.

The Pro's internal resolution is only slightly higher than the standard PS5's, and it doesn't appear to use [[PSSR]] at launch, so most of the upgrade is lighting rather than sharpness. A 2026 patch added the upgraded PSSR 2.
The Pro's Performance mode reaches 60fps with some drops in demanding scenes.

reviews.headline: 1800p / 4K native · rock-solid 60fps
reviews.overview: DF calls Split Fiction one of the best-optimized games in recent times, especially impressive for an Unreal Engine 5 game. Oliver Mackenzie says there is nothing to criticize from a technical point of view.

findings.text: Both consoles hold a rock-solid 60 frames per second, even with two players on screen at once.

The standard PS5 renders at a [[native|Native resolution]] 1800p and the PS5 Pro at a native 4K, smoothed with [[TAA|TAA (temporal AA)]]. Rendering natively at such high resolutions is rare for a modern game, and it gives a very clean image.

Hazelight avoided Unreal Engine 5's demanding [[Lumen]] and [[Nanite]] features. Environments are kept contained and global illumination is [[baked|Baked lighting / lightmaps]], which is how the game achieves both high resolution and a locked frame rate.

reviews.headline: 3 modes · blurry textures · runs better than beta
reviews.overview: DF found Monster Hunter Wilds runs considerably better than its open beta, and each mode mostly hits its target. But the visuals fall short of their potential, with blurry textures and uneven lighting, so the world may look less spectacular than fans hoped.

findings.text: All three modes generally hit their targets, and Prioritize Framerate is the smoothest with a 60fps cap. Because the PS5 lacks [[low framerate compensation|LFC (low framerate compensation)]], drops below the [[VRR window|VRR window]] can still feel choppy.
Lighting is uneven. Objects in direct sunlight look vivid, but much of the map looks dim and grainy, with odd reflections.
[[Textures|Texture resolution]] look blurry in the other modes, which may push some players toward 30 or 40fps for better visuals.

findings.title: Upgraded PSSR on PS5 Pro (2026)
findings.text: After the March 2026 [[PSSR]] upgrade on [[PS5 Pro|PS5 Pro]], [[anti-aliasing|Anti-aliasing (AA)]] is noticeably better, reflections are more stable and fine detail holds together better, especially in the 60fps performance mode.

reviews.headline: 60fps on all PS5s · PSSR on Pro
reviews.overview: DF calls Kingdom Come: Deliverance II a technical powerhouse on PS5 Pro. Unlike the first game on PS4, it reaches 60 frames per second on every PS5, and the Pro delivers quality-mode visuals at a performance-mode frame rate.

findings.text: Every PS5 owner can play at 60 frames per second, a big change from the first game, which struggled to run well on PS4.
The [[PS5 Pro]] uses its extra power and [[PSSR]] upscaling well. DF says it delivers what Sony promised for the Pro: fidelity-mode visuals at a performance-mode frame rate.
DF says the long wait for the sequel was well worth it from a technical point of view.

reviews.headline: 1080p/30 RT or 720p/60 (down to 504p)
reviews.overview: DF found Dragon Age: The Veilguard visually impressive with good performance on PS5. The 60fps mode relies on a very low internal resolution, but DF says it doesn't hurt the overall image as much as you'd expect.

findings.text: Performance mode consistently hits its 60 frames per second target.

Quality mode renders at 1080p and upscales to 4K with a custom version of [[FSR]] 2.2. Performance mode renders at 720p, upscales to 1440p, and uses [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] that can fall as low as 504p. The low resolution is noticeable up close, but the image still holds together well.
Quality mode turns on [[ray-traced reflections|RT reflections]] and [[ray-traced ambient occlusion|RTAO]]. The later [[PS5 Pro]] version adds ray-traced ambient occlusion to its 60fps mode as well.

findings.title: Upgraded PSSR on PS5 Pro (2026)
findings.text: With the March 2026 [[PSSR]] upgrade on [[PS5 Pro|PS5 Pro]], foliage looks better and upscaling errors are reduced. DF described the gains as visible, though not dramatic.

reviews.headline: 30 / 40 / 60fps · all hit target
reviews.overview: John Linneman says the changes are so significant that he isn't sure "remaster" is even the right word. DF considers the $10 upgrade completely fair and compares the work to Bluepoint's Shadow of the Colossus and Demon's Souls remakes, if not quite as ambitious.

findings.text: There are three modes targeting 30, 40 and 60 frames per second, and DF found that all three hit their targets perfectly. The 40fps [[Balanced mode]] needs a 120Hz display.

All three modes use [[dynamic resolution scaling|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]]. Quality mode aims for [[native|Native resolution]] 4K, while the other two stay below 1800p. In practice, the modes look very similar, and DF thinks Performance mode's image is good enough to recommend it to most players.

Terrain is far more detailed than in the 2017 original. [[Foliage|Alpha-tested foliage]] has been substantially revamped and now reacts as Aloy moves through it. Character models keep roughly the same [[polygon count|Polygons / triangles]], but skin and hair are much more realistic, which DF calls downright transformative.
Lighting has been improved across the world. Water rendering, especially its reflections, is a particular highlight, though it still isn't as good as in Horizon Forbidden West.
New motion capture brings the simpler dialogue scenes to life. Together with the visual changes, DF sees this as much closer to a [[remake|Remaster / remake]] than a typical remaster.

reviews.headline: ~1656p · 60fps target, no AA
reviews.overview: DF called Metaphor a sublime game let down by bizarre technical choices: no anti-aliasing at all, an unsteady 60fps mode, and no 30fps quality option.

findings.text: Resolution isn't the problem. The game has no [[anti-aliasing|Anti-aliasing (AA)]] at all, so the detailed geometry and outline shaders create heavy [[shimmering|Shimmering / specular aliasing]]. DF felt only a [[temporal AA|TAA (temporal AA)]] solution would fix it.

There is only a 60fps mode and it doesn't hold its target consistently. DF found the PS4 Pro version, running on PS5, was one way to get a steadier experience, and the [[PS5 Pro|PS5 Pro]] can nearly lock it to 60.

A [[120Hz mode|120Hz mode]] output works, but the game lacks [[low framerate compensation|LFC (low framerate compensation)]], so [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] can't smooth the drops below its range.

reviews.headline: 864p–1152p · often ~45fps
reviews.overview: DF calls Bloober Team's remake an authentic Unreal Engine 5 recreation that looks great, but performance on PS5 is a real weak point. Even at a low internal resolution, the Performance mode often runs well below 60 frames per second.

findings.text: Performance mode targets 60 frames per second but many areas run at around 45, and one courtyard scene drops to 37. Later areas hold 60 more often. The game's thick fog and foliage are the main causes, and detailed interiors also cause drops.

Both modes use [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]]. Quality mode usually sits between 1224p and 1512p, while Performance mode ranges from 864p to 1152p and in the worst cases falls just above 720p.
The game uses Unreal Engine 5's [[Lumen]] lighting, and its dense [[volumetric fog|Volumetric lighting / fog]] is central to the look, which is also why it's so demanding.
DF's later look at the [[PS5 Pro]] found the upgrades unclear overall, with [[PSSR]] problems in the Quality mode. After patch 1.06, the Pro's Performance mode actually looked better.

reviews.game: The Legend of Zelda: Echoes of Wisdom
reviews.headline: 720–1080p · 60fps drops to 30 outdoors
reviews.overview: DF says Echoes of Wisdom does a lot right, and its experimental gameplay may outweigh its problems, but its frame rate is even worse than Link's Awakening. John Linneman concluded that the Switch badly needed a successor.

findings.text: Standing still in the overworld, the game holds 60 frames per second even when you move the camera. As soon as Zelda starts walking, it drops almost instantly to as low as 30. DF believes this is because the game constantly loads new level data as you move. Dungeons and smaller areas also drop frames, but far less severely.
Indoors, the docked resolution reaches 1080p, but in the overworld it falls to 720p. When you first step outside, the game shows a few frames at 1080p before dropping, just like Link's Awakening.
The overworld is bigger and more seamless than Link's Awakening's, which is part of why it pushes the original Switch even harder. The Switch 2 free update later fixed the frame rate.

reviews.headline: 1440p–4K · 60fps 99.99% of the time
reviews.overview: John Linneman calls Astro Bot's technical execution practically flawless. It blends technology, design and creativity almost perfectly, and DF strongly encourages everyone to play it.

findings.text: The game holds 60 frames per second 99.99% of the time. In DF's testing there was just one negligible drop, to 56fps, during a moment packed with visual effects and [[physics|Physics / destruction]] objects.

Resolution [[changes dynamically|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] between 1440p and full 4K. Even at the low end, the image stays clean, helped by the game's simple, bold visual design and very effective [[anti-aliasing|Anti-aliasing (AA)]] that leaves no visible artifacts.
DF describes it as a near-perfect result from Team Asobi. A later PS5 Pro patch improved it further.

reviews.headline: 720p–1620p · RT in every mode · 40fps best
reviews.overview: DF calls Star Wars Outlaws a standout Snowdrop engine effort, generally excellent on PS5 and rivaling Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora for detail and effects. Some compromises are unavoidable, and DF picks the 40fps mode as the best balance.

findings.text: Quality mode is mostly a stable 30 frames per second with occasional dips. Performance mode targets 60 but falls to around 50 in cities and open areas, which [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] can help hide. The 40fps Quality mode, available on 120Hz screens, is DF's recommended sweet spot.

[[Dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] ranges from 720p up to 1620p, and [[FSR]] upscales the image to between roughly 1440p and 4K. That leaves some artifacts, but DF says they don't hurt the overall image much.

[[Ray tracing|Ray tracing (RT)]] is active in every mode on console, including [[ray-traced global illumination|RTGI]]. Quality mode adds denser vegetation and a longer [[draw distance|Draw distance]].
The later [[PS5 Pro]] update offers a single mode that DF describes as the best of both worlds.

reviews.headline: Excellent visuals · too many tech problems
reviews.overview: DF found Black Myth: Wukong visually excellent on PS5 but with too many technical problems, calling it a PC-first game with a long patching road ahead. The biggest issue is that the 60fps mode uses frame generation, so it feels like a 30fps game.

findings.text: Performance mode uses [[frame generation|Frame generation]] to turn roughly 30 real frames per second into 60, which creates visible artifacts. Because only 30 frames are real, it [[responds like a 30fps game|Base frame rate]] despite looking smoother, and [[input latency|Input latency / input lag]] is DF's main complaint. It still drops into the 40s in combat. Balanced mode targets about 45fps with better input response, and Quality mode hovers around 31 to 36fps, falling into the 20s in fights.

There's no 120Hz mode and no proper [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] support, and the Quality and Balanced modes fall below the PS5's 48Hz VRR floor anyway. There's also no [[HDR|HDR (high dynamic range)]], and blacks never look truly black.

Quality mode moves between 1296p and 1584p using [[FSR]]. It looks fine in still frames but poor in motion, with weak [[anti-aliasing|Anti-aliasing (AA)]] and [[dithering|Dithering]]. Performance mode runs at 1080p with heavy [[sharpening|Sharpening]] that DF says makes the image look fried.
[[Lumen]] global illumination looks somewhat more refined in Quality mode.

reviews.headline: 4K/30, 1440p/60 or balanced 4K/60
reviews.overview: Even from the demo, DF found Stellar Blade technically strong across all its modes, with a lot of quality to celebrate, especially its bombastic in-engine cutscenes. The weak spots are some low-resolution background textures and the lack of ray tracing.

findings.text: Performance mode holds a steady 60 frames per second. The default Balanced mode also targets 60 and mostly hits it, with brief dips into the 50s that a [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] display smooths over. The Resolution mode holds 30fps.

Resolution mode renders at a [[native|Native resolution]] 4K, trimming a little image quality in busy scenes to protect its frame rate. Balanced mode [[reconstructs|Temporal upscaling / reconstruction]] a clean 4K image at 60fps, which is why DF recommends it. Performance mode renders at 1440p.
There is no ray tracing in any mode. Reflections use [[screen-space reflections|Screen-space reflections (SSR)]], so they can disappear when the reflected object leaves the screen.
Some background [[textures|Texture resolution]] are noticeably low-resolution, the main visual blemish DF found.
The in-engine cutscenes are the standout, running in real time rather than as video, so they keep the same sharpness as gameplay. The game was later ported to Switch 2 in 2026.

reviews.headline: ~936p · can't hold 60fps
reviews.overview: DF enjoyed Rise of the Ronin as a game, with good story, combat and RPG systems, but found it unconvincing technically. No mode delivers a solid 60 frames per second, and much of the presentation looks closer to the previous console generation.

findings.text: Performance mode targets 60 frames per second but often sits around 50 and dips to about 45. Quality mode is capped at 30 but suffers from poor [[frame pacing|Frame pacing]], so it feels less smooth than a good 30fps game should. With [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] and the cap removed, Quality mode reaches 40 to 50fps in lighter scenes. DF still recommends Performance mode for an action game.

Performance mode averages around 936p and upscales to 4K with [[FSR]] 2, which looks soft and introduces artifacts. Quality mode reaches 1512p but often falls to around 1152p. The ray-tracing mode averages just 810 to 900p.

NPCs [[pop in|Pop-in]] aggressively, which is especially noticeable in cities and on horseback. Low [[anisotropic filtering|Anisotropic filtering (AF)]] makes some surfaces look blurry, and vegetation quality is weak.

Shadows hold up well across the day-night cycle, but DF criticizes the overall lighting and [[shadow map|Shadow maps]] quality. Character models are detailed, and the linear missions have some impressive effects, but the open world often looks last-generation.

reviews.headline: Checkerboard 4K · 30–45fps · CPU-bound
reviews.overview: DF called Dragon's Dogma 2 a great graphical achievement let down by its console configuration. It runs at a checkerboarded 4K with no frame-rate cap and no graphics options, so performance swings widely, and Capcom simply must improve it.

findings.text: The frame rate usually sits between 30 and 45 frames per second with no cap, and it is much worse in busy areas. There's no Performance mode or graphics menu at all on PS5.
The game uses [[checkerboard rendering|Checkerboard rendering (CBR)]] to reach 4K, and the visuals are generally strong.
DF praised the [[ray-traced global illumination|RTGI]].
To save processor time, NPC [[draw distance|Draw distance]] is reduced on PS5, so townsfolk can [[pop in|Pop-in]] very close to you.

The game is heavily [[CPU-bound|CPU-bound / CPU-limited]]. Towns full of NPCs and fights with many enemies cause the biggest drops, because the processor can't keep up with simulating them, so lowering resolution wouldn't help much.

findings.title: Upgraded PSSR on PS5 Pro (2026)
findings.text: In DF's March 2026 round-up of upgraded [[PSSR]] on [[PS5 Pro|PS5 Pro]], Dragon's Dogma 2 was one of the games where issues remain, with visible dot patterns in the image even though the picture is better overall.

reviews.headline: 4K / 30 or soft ~1152p / 60
reviews.overview: DF calls Final Fantasy VII Rebirth an excellent but inconsistent experience. The open world, towns and cities are impressive in Graphics mode, but the 60fps Performance mode looks noticeably soft and blocky, and falls short of Final Fantasy VII Remake.

findings.text: Graphics mode usually renders at or near 4K. Performance mode averages around 1152p, lower than the 1512p of Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade, and its upscaling appears to simply double pixels in a [[nearest-neighbour style|Spatial upscaling]]. The result is a blocky, slightly soft image that doesn't look much sharper than ordinary scaling, which is the biggest reason DF calls Performance mode disappointing.
Some lighting is visibly wrong in places, and several traversal animations look off. Even so, the more detailed cities, towns and open areas look impressive.
Some items use low-resolution models, and characters clip straight through [[foliage|Alpha-tested foliage]] instead of brushing it aside.
DF later found that the [[PS5 Pro]] patch delivers a night-and-day improvement to the 60fps mode, fixing much of its image-quality problem.

findings.title: Upgraded PSSR on PS5 Pro (2026)
findings.text: DF retested the game after Sony's March 2026 [[PSSR]] upgrade. Edges are better defined, [[aliasing|Aliasing / jaggies]] is reduced both in motion and when standing still, and foliage looks more convincing. The 60fps mode on [[PS5 Pro|PS5 Pro]] now looks comparable to the standard PS5's quality mode.

reviews.headline: 864–1260p/60 or 1296–1800p/30 · full RT
reviews.overview: DF called Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora one of the most impressive games of the year, and a pretty impressive package on consoles. It uses a full suite of ray tracing even on PS5, and scales gracefully from its maxed-out PC version.

findings.text: Both modes include [[ray-traced global illumination|RTGI]] and [[ray-traced reflections|RT reflections]], lower in quality than the top PC settings but still unusual for a console game.

Both modes use [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] upscaled to 4K with [[FSR]] 2. The PS5 often sits slightly lower in its range than the Xbox Series X, but the Xbox shows more noticeable reconstruction artifacts.

Performance mode mostly holds 50 to 60 frames per second but can dip to the mid-40s. Quality mode is a much steadier 30, and the Xbox showed traversal hitching the PS5 didn't. The reviewer preferred Quality mode for its sharper image and more consistent performance.
DF later found the [[PS5 Pro]] update disappointing.

reviews.headline: 1080p docked / 720p handheld · 60fps
reviews.overview: DF called the Super Mario RPG remake almost perfect technically: full 1080p docked, 720p handheld, and nearly always 60 frames per second.

findings.text: The game renders at the full [[native resolution|Native resolution]] of each mode, so it looks sharp and clean on both the TV and the handheld screen.
It is nearly always at 60 frames per second. The rare drops are brief, but because the game is usually so smooth, they show up as a jarring [[stutter|Stutter / hitch]] when they happen.
DF felt this was a model remake: a modest visual style chosen to fit the hardware, leaving enough headroom to keep it smooth.

reviews.headline: 1272p/30 or 872p/60 · FSR 2
reviews.overview: DF found Alan Wake 2 on PS5 fairly solid, with geometry and detail quite comparable to a maxed-out PC. But Remedy is clearly straining the hardware: internal resolutions are low, and ray tracing is missing entirely.

findings.text: Quality mode mostly holds 30 frames per second, dipping by a few frames outdoors. Performance mode holds 60 indoors and falls to around 50 in some outdoor areas. That's still a big improvement over how Control ran on consoles.

Quality mode renders at 1272p and upscales to 4K with [[FSR]] 2. Performance mode renders at just 872p and upscales to 1440p, with noticeable [[aliasing|Aliasing / jaggies]]. The later [[PS5 Pro]] version still renders at 864p for 60fps, using [[PSSR]] to clean it up, and DF called the 2026 [[PSSR]] 2 update a great showcase.
The PS5 has no [[ray-traced reflections|RT reflections]] or [[path tracing|Path tracing (PT)]], so reflections and shadows are a clear step below the PC version.

reviews.headline: 1440p–4K/30 or 1008–1440p/60 · world-class RT
reviews.overview: DF called Spider-Man 2's ray-traced reflections the best of any open-world console game, with nothing else coming close. Both main modes run well, and DF favored the 60fps Performance mode.

findings.text: Performance mode holds 60 frames per second most of the time, dipping occasionally in dense areas. Fidelity is capped at 30 and fairly stable. On a 120Hz display, Fidelity can run at 40fps, and with [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] and the cap removed, Performance mode reaches 65 to 80fps.

Both modes use [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] and Insomniac's temporal injection upscaler to reach a 4K output. Fidelity ranges from 1440p to 2160p internally, and Performance from 1008p to 1440p. The visual gap between the two is bigger than in Insomniac's earlier PS5 games, with denser vegetation and more detail in Fidelity.

[[Ray-traced reflections|RT reflections]] appear in both modes, and DF calls them the best in any open-world console game, with nothing else coming close. Fidelity mode uses ray tracing more widely, including on water, which is part of why it is heavier.

findings.title: QSSR on standard PS5 (November 2026)
findings.text: A free update released in November 2026 adds [[QSSR]], Sony's AI upscaler for the standard PS5, to both Fidelity and Performance modes. Insomniac says it makes the image more stable and sharper. It's the same studio's second QSSR game after Wolverine, where DF found a big gain in detail for a cost of about 8 to 10 frames per second. DF hasn't published test results for Spider-Man 2 yet, so this is the developer's description.

reviews.headline: 1080p · near-flawless 60fps
reviews.overview: DF calls Super Mario Bros. Wonder an excellent showcase for the Switch. It doesn't push technical boundaries, but it benefits from focusing on what it wants to do and executing it extremely well.

findings.text: The game runs at a near-flawless 60 frames per second with only rare dips. There are occasional brief [[stutters|Stutter / hitch]] when entering levels, but they don't affect play.

Docked, it renders at 1080p and uses [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] to drop as low as 864p when needed, which DF notes is relatively uncommon for a 2D Mario game. Handheld renders 720p.

The game is full of animation detail. Mario and enemies track each other with their eyes, enemies react to what Mario does, and stages transform with dynamic shadows and cartoonish [[particle effects|Particles]], all at a near-locked 60fps.

reviews.headline: 648p–1152p 60fps perf / ~1296p–1620p 30fps quality
reviews.overview: DF described Lords of the Fallen as a stunning-looking reboot with ongoing technical issues. PS5 had the edge over Series X in performance mode, but both consoles drop resolution heavily and still dip below 60.

findings.text: Performance mode uses aggressive [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]], falling as low as 648p, which makes the image soft on a big TV.
Performance mode frequently dips below 60 frames per second and has [[stutter|Stutter / hitch]], though DF found PS5 ran it better than Series X. Quality mode is locked at 30.
The game runs on [[Unreal Engine 5|Unreal Engine 5 (UE5)]], and DF saw it as an example of how demanding the engine's lighting is on consoles. Many patches followed launch to improve performance.

reviews.headline: Native 4K/30 · 1512–1800p/60 · well optimized
reviews.overview: DF considers Lies of P well optimized on every console, with the PS5 and Xbox Series X versions essentially equal. For a fast action game, they strongly recommend the 60fps Performance mode.

findings.text: Performance mode has consistent [[frame pacing|Frame pacing]] and stays smooth in nearly every situation. The 30fps Quality mode and the 40fps mode both hold their frame rates, but uneven frame pacing makes them feel less smooth than the numbers suggest.
Quality mode renders a fixed [[native|Native resolution]] 4K. The 40fps mode moves between 1872p and 4K, and Performance mode between 1512p and 1800p, smoothed with [[TAA|TAA (temporal AA)]].
Performance mode reduces [[volumetric fog|Volumetric lighting / fog]] and lighting quality to reach 60fps.

reviews.headline: 1008–1440p/60 · RT mode 1440p/30
reviews.overview: With version 2.0 and Phantom Liberty, DF found Cyberpunk 2077 considerably more solid on PS5 now that last-gen consoles are no longer supported, though the new Dogtown area still has shaky moments.

findings.text: In the original game areas, the PS5 mostly holds 60 frames per second in Performance mode, dipping only a couple of frames, which was steadier than the Xbox Series X. In Phantom Liberty's Dogtown, Performance mode often sits in the low-to-mid 50s. The Ray Tracing mode is locked to 30fps and more stable.
Performance mode uses [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] between 1008p and 1440p, upscaled to 1800p. Ray Tracing mode renders at 1440p and upscales to 4K.
The Ray Tracing mode adds [[ray-traced|Ray tracing (RT)]] effects at the cost of a 30fps cap.

reviews.headline: PC Ultra visuals · Act 3 drops to 20fps
reviews.overview: DF found that Baldur's Gate 3 on PS5 effectively matches the PC version at Ultra settings, which is impressive. Performance is the weak point, though: the crowded city of Act 3 drags the frame rate down to as low as 20 in both modes.

findings.text: In Acts 1 and 2, Quality mode holds a steady 30 frames per second and Performance mode mostly sits in the mid-to-high 50s. In Act 3 the city of Baldur's Gate, full of NPCs, drops Performance mode as low as 20fps, and the same problem happens on PC.

In Act 3, both modes perform about the same, a clear sign the game is [[CPU-bound|CPU-bound / CPU-limited]]: the processor can't simulate all those characters fast enough, so lowering resolution doesn't help.
Quality mode renders a locked 1440p. Performance mode renders around 960p and upscales with [[FSR]] 2. Split-screen co-op forces Quality mode at 30fps, splitting the screen into two 1280×1440 views.

reviews.headline: Dynamic 900p docked / 720p handheld · locked 30fps
reviews.overview: Pikmin 4 is the first game Nintendo built in-house with Unreal Engine, and DF counted it among the best-looking first-party Switch games, with clean visuals and a stable 30 frames per second.

findings.text: The garden and house settings have soft, natural lighting and realistic materials, which helps the tiny Pikmin feel like they are exploring a real backyard.
Unlike many Switch games, Pikmin 4 uses [[anti-aliasing|Anti-aliasing (AA)]], so edges are smoother and the image looks cleaner than its resolution suggests.
DF noted that Nintendo using an outside [[game engine|Game engine]] like Unreal for one of its own games was unusual, and that the results show the engine can run well on Switch with care.

reviews.headline: 1080–1440p/30 or down to 720p/60
reviews.overview: DF praised Final Fantasy XVI's art, cutscenes, characters and particle effects, but recommends the 30fps Quality mode, because the Performance mode's image falls apart while still failing to hold 60.

findings.text: Quality mode is locked at 30 frames per second. Performance mode stays consistently below 60 while exploring and only reaches 60 during combat, which is exactly when its resolution drops lowest.

Quality mode renders between 1080p and 1440p, and Performance mode can fall as low as 720p. DF believes Square Enix uses AMD's older [[FSR 1|FSR]], a [[spatial upscaler|Spatial upscaling]], which leaves the image blurry with visible artifacts. That's the main reason DF recommends Quality mode.

Indoor and dim scenes use [[baked lighting|Baked lighting / lightmaps]] and look great, but bright outdoor areas look like a step down, closer to a cross-generation game. Performance mode also has lower-quality shadows and more [[pop-in|Pop-in]].
The [[particle effects|Particles]] in the huge Eikon battles are a highlight.

reviews.game: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom
reviews.headline: ~900p docked · solid 30fps
reviews.overview: DF found that Tears of the Kingdom runs pretty darn well on Switch, a near miracle given its physics-based building on six-year-old hardware. Some areas need improvement, and the visuals fall short of the early trailers.

findings.text: After a patch fixed problems in the review build, the game ran at a solid 30 frames per second almost all of the time. Drops happen in busy moments like heavy Ultrahand building, but [[frame pacing|Frame pacing]] is smooth, with no significant stutter or hitching.

Docked resolution is about 900p but [[dynamic|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]], dropping to around 720p while the camera moves and returning to 900p when it stops. Handheld tops out at 720p, which DF says looks good on the Switch OLED screen.
Pre-rendered cutscenes have exceptionally poor video quality, while the real-time ones look much better. DF also praised the 5.1 surround sound and the new cloud system.

reviews.headline: 648–864p/60 · unstable at launch
reviews.overview: DF found Star Wars Jedi: Survivor's technical state on consoles rather unsatisfying at launch. Performance mode renders at around 720p and still can't hold 60 frames per second.

findings.text: Performance mode is unstable, with large swings down to about 45 frames per second. Quality mode sometimes drops below 30.
Performance mode renders between 648p and 864p and upscales to 1440p with [[FSR]] 2, which looks soft. Quality mode reaches up to 1440p, upscaled to 4K.
Without [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]], [[screen tearing|Screen tearing]] appears in the upper third of the image.
Patch 1.03 brought only marginal gains on PS5 at first; Respawn kept patching the game afterwards.

findings.title: Upgraded PSSR on PS5 Pro (2026)
findings.text: DF's March 2026 test of upgraded [[PSSR]] on [[PS5 Pro|PS5 Pro]] found the overall picture improved, but problems remain here: [[ray-traced reflections|RT reflections]] look sharp yet noisy in motion, and small dot patterns appear in the image.

reviews.headline: Checkerboard 4K · soft image at launch
reviews.overview: At launch, John Linneman found Resident Evil 4's PS5 version ran slightly faster than Xbox Series X but looked softer, with shimmering caused by a flawed checkerboard implementation. Patch 1.004 noticeably improved the PS5 image a few weeks later.

findings.text: Both modes use [[checkerboard rendering|Checkerboard rendering (CBR)]], at 2160p and 1944p. On PS5 the implementation looked flawed at launch, giving a softer image with [[shimmering|Shimmering / specular aliasing]] on objects. Patch 1.004 improved the reconstruction, giving a clearer look with some artifacts remaining, and removed the [[chromatic aberration|Chromatic aberration (CA)]].
The PS5 ran slightly faster than the Xbox Series X. With everything turned on (Resolution mode, ray tracing and strand-based hair), it runs in the upper 40s.

The launch build fixed the demo's limited [[ray-traced reflections|RT reflections]] on PS5, but the lighting on [[strand-based hair|Hair strands / hair cards]] was still broken. Patch 1.004 removed [[screen-space reflections|Screen-space reflections (SSR)]] with ray tracing off, falling back to older reflection methods.

reviews.headline: Dynamic 1440p/60 · stutter · 21 modes
reviews.overview: DF tested 21 mode combinations and found Hogwarts Legacy good-looking but flawed on PS5. Its performance is more stable than the Xbox Series X version at the same settings, but the 60fps mode still stutters often.

findings.text: Performance mode targets 60 frames per second with [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] up to 1440p, but drops and frequent [[stutter|Stutter / hitch]] remain, which [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] can soften. The 40fps Balanced mode hits its target with fewer problems than on Xbox. Unlocking the frame rate on a VRR display gains very little.

The Ray Tracing mode holds a stable 30fps at 1440p, but large water surfaces like lakes don't get ray-traced reflections. DF also found missing [[shadow maps|Shadow maps]] and [[light bleeding|Light leaking]].
Some textures flicker.

reviews.headline: 900p · locked 60fps · all-new assets
reviews.overview: DF calls Metroid Prime Remastered a more approachable and beautifully refined take on the GameCube original, and one of the best-looking games on Switch.

findings.text: The game holds a steady 60 frames per second in both modes, with no noticeable dips in DF's testing.

It renders at a fixed 900p docked and 600p handheld, with no dynamic resolution and no [[anti-aliasing|Anti-aliasing (AA)]]. That's unusual for a modern game, but DF says it isn't a major problem because the game has few real-time effects that would shimmer.
Every model and texture was remade, with higher [[polygon counts|Polygons / triangles]] and more detailed [[textures|Texture resolution]], while staying faithful to the original's style.
The revamped lighting looks especially good on the Switch OLED in handheld mode, where its dark tones stand out.

reviews.headline: 1440p/60 · best-in-class remake
reviews.overview: DF called EA Motive's Dead Space a best-in-class remake, on par with Resident Evil 2 and 3. It runs at a stable 60 frames per second on PS5, though a rendering bug made dark areas look pixelated until it was patched.

findings.text: Performance mode holds a stable 60 frames per second at a 1440p target, while Quality mode targets 4K at 30.

At launch, the PS5's variable rate shading, a technique that renders less important parts of the image in less detail, wasn't working as intended, causing heavy [[pixelation|Aliasing / jaggies]] in the darkest parts of the frame. A patch fixed it.
Shadows are used masterfully in the near-darkness, and [[volumetric lighting|Volumetric lighting / fog]] cuts effective shafts of light through the gloom.
A full [[remake|Remaster / remake]] rebuilt on the Frostbite engine.

reviews.headline: Down to 720p/60 · Quality drops to 20fps
reviews.overview: DF found Forspoken on PS5 a mixed technical package. Loading is lightning fast and characters look great, but the Quality mode can't hold 30 frames per second, which DF called simply absurd, and lighting is a step back even from Final Fantasy XV.

findings.text: Performance mode mostly holds 60 frames per second but dips well below 50 in some open-world areas. Quality mode can't hold 30 and drops to around 20 at times.
Performance mode uses [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] that can fall as low as 720p.
DF called the lighting a significant step back, even compared with Final Fantasy XV.
Loading is extremely fast, about four seconds from the title screen and under a second when continuing a save, thanks to the PS5's [[SSD|SSD / NVMe]].
Animation, [[particle effects|Particles]], character models and hair physics are all strong points.

reviews.headline: Best console version · RT reflections
reviews.overview: DF called the PS5 version of The Callisto Protocol a simply brilliant game and a proper technical showcase, and the best way to play at launch. The Xbox Series X version struggled in its Quality mode, and the PC version stuttered badly.

findings.text: The PS5 version has [[ray-traced reflections|RT reflections]], which the Xbox Series X version lacked at launch, and ray tracing adds noticeable depth to the dark environments.

Both modes run well on PS5. By comparison, the Xbox Series X suffered huge frame-rate drops in Quality mode, and the PC version had what DF called unbelievably bad [[shader compilation stutter|Shader compilation stutter]].
DF singled out the PS5 as the smoothest way to play at launch.

reviews.headline: Can't hold 30fps · "technical failures"
reviews.overview: DF called Pokémon Scarlet and Violet comprehensive technical failures on the original Switch. Even with heavily pared-back visuals, they can't hold 30 frames per second, and pop-in and choppy distant animation make exploring unpleasant. The Switch 2 update later fixed much of this.

findings.text: The games dip and stutter often while moving through open areas, and still can't hold 30 frames per second despite their simple visuals.
NPCs [[pop in|Pop-in]] suddenly in towns, and distant characters and objects [[animate|Half-rate animation]] at 2 frames per second or lower, which DF calls highly distracting.
Docked image quality is described as questionable, and artwork and textures often look ugly and cheap, falling short even of Pokémon Legends: Arceus.

reviews.headline: ~1872p/60 · flawless performance
reviews.overview: John Linneman described the PS5 version as like a maxed-out PC port with flawless performance: effectively no stutters, hitches or bugs. It isn't pushing the technology envelope, but it is a natural, polished evolution of the 2018 game.

findings.text: DF saw effectively no stutters or hitches in any mode. Performance mode is a locked 60 frames per second. With a [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] display, the high frame rate mode removes the cap and typically runs at 80 to 90fps. Quality mode can also run as a locked 40fps on 120Hz screens.
Quality mode targets native 4K and rarely dips to around 1800p. Performance mode usually sits around 1872p, which still looks sharp on a 4K TV.

Quality mode adds sharper, contact-hardened shadows, a shadow from Kratos's axe, better [[ambient occlusion|Ambient occlusion (AO)]] and more [[distant detail|Level of detail (LOD)]], so it is more than a resolution change. DF still favors the 60fps mode unless you have a VRR TV for the 40fps option.

reviews.headline: Dynamic 810p docked / ~480p handheld · unstable 60
reviews.overview: DF was disappointed by Bayonetta 3's performance. It aims for 60 frames per second but rarely holds it, the resolution drops very low in handheld, and DF ranked it below every other Bayonetta release except the original PS3 version.

findings.text: The game targets 60 frames per second but spends much of its time below it, and some large set pieces are capped at 30. For a fast action game where timing dodges matters, that instability is a real problem.
[[Dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] keeps docked around 810p, while handheld can fall to roughly 480p, which looks very [[soft|Soft / blurry image]] on the screen.
Many [[textures|Texture resolution]] look muddy, which DF saw as another sign the game was pushing the Switch beyond what it could comfortably handle.

reviews.headline: ~1080p docked / up to 720p handheld · 60fps battles
reviews.overview: DF found Splatoon 3 keeps the series' locked 60 frames per second in battle, which matters most for an online shooter, while the image quality is fairly soft and the town hub runs at 30.

findings.text: Turf battles are [[locked|Locked / capped]] at 60 frames per second, which keeps aiming responsive. The social hub runs at 30, which matters less because you are just walking around.

Both modes use [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]]. The game uses [[FSR|FSR]] 1, a simple [[spatial upscaler|Spatial upscaling]], but DF found it added little because there is no [[anti-aliasing|Anti-aliasing (AA)]] to smooth the edges first.
Loading into matches takes under 10 seconds, a nice improvement for a game where you jump in and out of short rounds.

reviews.game: The Last of Us Part I
reviews.headline: Every asset rebuilt · 60fps+ with VRR
reviews.overview: DF called The Last of Us Part I as complete a remake as you could hope for, and a technical marvel. Every asset was rebuilt from scratch, and on a 120Hz VRR display the frame rate can go above 60.

findings.text: Every asset was remade from scratch, with much higher [[geometric detail|Polygons / triangles]], new materials, smoother edges and new background structures.

Characters were completely refreshed, with more natural skin, facial hair, eyes and clothing. Cutscene direction, [[depth of field|Depth of field (DOF)]] and [[motion blur|Per-object motion blur]] are improved, often matching or beating The Last of Us Part II.
Shading and lighting were rebuilt and water reflections look better, though there's no ray tracing.
With the frame rate unlocked on a 120Hz [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] display, the PS5 can run above 60 frames per second, and DF says performance stays strong throughout.
Joel has no new moves, but animation, camera work and enemy behavior were substantially reworked, so this is a full [[remake|Remaster / remake]] rather than a remaster.

reviews.headline: ~540p base · 30fps · sharper than XC2
reviews.overview: DF found Xenoblade Chronicles 3 a clear improvement over Xenoblade Chronicles 2, and one of the sharper high-end Switch games in handheld mode, though pop-in and some image breakup remain.

findings.text: The game is capped at 30 frames per second with correct [[frame pacing|Frame pacing]]. Performance varies with the complexity of the scene and the size of battles, while cutscenes run at or near 30.

The most common internal resolution is about 540p, but the game appears to use [[temporal upsampling|Temporal upscaling / reconstruction]] to build a more detailed final image. That helps a lot, though DF still saw some breakup and subtle warbling in motion.
View distances are long, but rocks, trees and grass [[pop in|Pop-in]] as you travel, though less jarringly than in earlier Xenoblade games.
The sky combines a textured dome with a procedural cloud system that changes with the weather. Shadows don't shift with the sun's position.

reviews.headline: Up to 1080p docked / 720p handheld · 30fps
reviews.overview: John Linneman praised Kirby's first full 3D adventure for its looks and stability, but his main criticism was the 30 frames per second target, especially compared with Super Mario Odyssey's 60.

findings.text: Docked uses [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]], reaching 1080p at best and dipping to around 810p in busier scenes. Handheld sits at 720p.
The game holds its 30fps target well, but DF felt a 3D platformer like this would feel much better at 60, which is what Mario Odyssey offered on the same hardware.

Enemies and objects in the distance animate at a reduced rate, a trick called [[half-rate animation|Half-rate animation]]. It saves processing time but makes faraway characters look choppy next to Kirby.

reviews.headline: 45–60fps · no stable 60 · PS4 version trick
reviews.overview: At launch, DF found Elden Ring's console performance a mixed bag. Neither PS5 mode holds a stable 60 frames per second, and oddly, the PS4 version running on PS5 was the smoothest way to play.

findings.text: The frame-rate mode bounces between 45 and 60. The quality mode is unlocked and swings between 30 and 60, and DF said a locked 30fps option would have been better. Performance was practically unchanged from the beta.
Running the PS4 version through [[backwards compatibility|Backwards compatibility]] holds a steady 60fps, at the cost of lower resolution and visual quality.
At the time, PS5 had no [[VRR|VRR (variable refresh rate)]] support to smooth out the drops.
DF later found that even the [[PS5 Pro]] can't hold a stable 60fps in Elden Ring.

reviews.headline: Native 4K/30 or 1800p CB/60
reviews.overview: DF found Horizon Forbidden West essentially locked in both modes, and a big leap over Horizon Zero Dawn. At launch they recommended the 30fps Resolution mode, because the 60fps mode gave up a sizeable part of the visual experience.

findings.text: Both modes are essentially locked, and DF had trouble finding any frame drops on PS5. There's occasional stutter on camera cuts, and cutscenes are less stable in Performance mode.

Resolution mode renders a [[native|Native resolution]] 4K. Performance mode uses [[checkerboard rendering|Checkerboard rendering (CBR)]] at 1800p, rendering half the pixels each frame and reconstructing the rest. At launch this made it noticeably softer, which is why DF recommended Resolution mode. Later patches improved Performance mode a lot.
Compared with the PS4 version, the PS5 has much denser geometry, higher-quality assets and better foliage.

reviews.headline: 900p–1080p docked / ~720p handheld · 30fps
reviews.overview: DF's take was that Legends: Arceus is fun to play but technically rough, with plain visuals and performance that could be better, especially when docked.

findings.text: Handheld holds a solid 30 frames per second, but docked has more [[hitches|Stutter / hitch]], so handheld is the smoother way to play.
The open areas look sparse, with simple [[textures|Texture resolution]] and visible [[pop-in|Pop-in]] as objects and Pokémon appear close to the player.
DF praised the new gameplay ideas but said the visuals and performance fall short of what other Switch open-world games had already achieved.

reviews.headline: 4K 30fps quality / 1080p 60fps performance
reviews.overview: DF found a big gap between the two modes and recommended the quality mode on PS5, because the performance mode drops resolution and effects heavily and still doesn't hold 60.

findings.text: Performance mode targets 60 frames per second but doesn't always reach it, with dips reported as low as the 40s, so the trade-off isn't as good as it sounds.
Quality mode holds 4K with better [[anti-aliasing|Anti-aliasing (AA)]], while performance mode drops to 1080p, a big step down on a 4K TV.
Quality mode also has better [[shadows|Shadow maps]] and denser foliage. A later patch added a [[ray tracing|Ray tracing (RT)]] mode, which DF covered separately.

reviews.headline: 900p docked / 720p handheld · 60fps
reviews.overview: DF called Metroid Dread one of the best-looking 2.5D games around. It trades raw sharpness for a fast, mostly steady 60 frames per second, which matters a lot in a game built on quick dodges and counters.

findings.text: Gameplay runs at a mostly steady 60 frames per second in both modes, with only rare slowdown. Cutscenes drop to 30, which is a common trade-off because cinematic shots use heavier lighting and effects, and the switch between the two rates is noticeable but brief.

Docked renders at 900p and is upscaled to 1080p for the TV, while handheld matches the screen at 720p. There is no [[anti-aliasing|Anti-aliasing (AA)]], so edges show some [[jaggies|Aliasing / jaggies]], although the strong art direction keeps the image looking clean overall.
DF's view is that MercurySteam spent its budget where it counts: lighting, detailed backgrounds and animation, while keeping the 60fps target that the combat design depends on.

reviews.headline: Native 4K or 1800p · 60fps · ~6s loads
reviews.overview: DF found the PS5 Director's Cut a polished upgrade: every mode targets 60 frames per second, including a new ultrawide option, and loading drops from about a minute to a few seconds.

findings.text: All three modes target 60 frames per second. Performance mode holds it consistently, while quality mode occasionally dips into the 50s in some cutscenes and heavy combat.
Quality mode renders at full [[native|Native resolution]] 4K, performance mode at 1800p upscaled to 4K. The ultrawide mode renders a cinematic 21:9 image with black bars.
Thanks to the [[SSD|SSD / NVMe]], loading into the game takes about 6 seconds instead of roughly a minute on PS4.

Some character [[textures|Texture resolution]] are upgraded, and draw distance, water and foliage are improved, though environments are mostly unchanged. [[Texture filtering|Texture filtering]] is still noticeably weak.

reviews.headline: 4K · 60fps · sub-4s loads
reviews.overview: DF found the PS5 Director's Cut is mostly the original game run faster and sharper: 4K at a stable 60 frames per second, with loading cut to a few seconds by the SSD.

findings.text: The PS5 version runs at a stable 60 frames per second, double the original PS4 target, which makes the sword combat feel noticeably more responsive.
Loading takes under 4 seconds at most thanks to the [[SSD|SSD / NVMe]], a dramatic change from the long PS4 loads.
Some objects received slightly better [[textures|Texture resolution]], but otherwise the visuals are the same. Sucker Punch didn't add new lighting techniques or [[ray tracing|Ray tracing (RT)]].
Some pre-rendered cutscenes were replaced with real-time ones, so they now match the gameplay's sharpness instead of being compressed video.

reviews.headline: Mostly 60fps with RT · loads in ~1s
reviews.overview: DF found Capcom transitioned beautifully to the new consoles with Resident Evil Village. Even with ray tracing on, the PS5 mostly holds 60 frames per second, and it loads almost instantly.

findings.text: Capcom's own estimate of 45fps with ray tracing turned out to be pessimistic: the PS5 holds 60 most of the time. The main exception is Moreau's Reservoir in the second half, where it drops to the mid-40s, slightly below the Xbox Series X.
The game supports [[ray tracing|Ray tracing (RT)]], without costing as much frame rate as expected.
Loading is a big PS5 advantage: the game starts almost instantly with about a one-second cut to black, compared with roughly 8.5 seconds on Xbox Series X.

reviews.headline: 1080p → 4K · mostly 60fps
reviews.overview: DF found Returnal visually rich with generally great performance. It technically outputs a dynamic 4K, but the native resolution is only around 1080p, rebuilt in two steps.

findings.text: The game mostly holds 60 frames per second, with brief dips into the mid-to-low 50s.

Housemarque renders at around 1080p, uses [[temporal upsampling|Temporal upscaling / reconstruction]] to reach 1440p, then [[checkerboard rendering|Checkerboard rendering (CBR)]] to reach 4K. That double upscale can make the image look a bit grainy at times.
Ray tracing is used mostly behind the scenes, to make rendering more efficient and to improve 3D audio.

reviews.headline: 1080p / 720p · 30fps
reviews.overview: DF found Animal Crossing: New Horizons relatively smooth and good-looking. It drops to 30 frames per second, half the GameCube original's 60, but DF considers that a worthy sacrifice for the visual upgrade.

findings.text: The game runs at 30 frames per second in both modes, with only a few minor blips. Earlier entries on GameCube and Wii ran at 60.
It renders at a full 1080p docked and 720p handheld, but [[anti-aliasing|Anti-aliasing (AA)]] is practically absent, so edges look [[jagged|Aliasing / jaggies]].
[[Bloom]] and [[ambient occlusion|Ambient occlusion (AO)]] add softness and depth, and the pop-in of earlier games appears to be solved.
DF believes it runs on the same in-house Nintendo [[engine|Game engine]] as ARMS, Splatoon 2 and Super Mario Maker 2, sharing their lighting and material techniques.

reviews.headline: Dynamic 864p–1080p docked / 576p–720p handheld · 30fps
reviews.overview: DF found Sword and Shield technically underwhelming: the frame rate dips in battles, the pop-in is extreme, and the textures are poor, even by Switch standards.

findings.text: The game targets 30 frames per second but falls into the 20s when entering battles and during Dynamax moves, the very moments meant to feel exciting.

[[Pop-in|Pop-in]] in the Wild Area is extreme, with objects and Pokémon appearing just in front of the player, which DF described as almost comical. Many [[textures|Texture resolution]] are low quality.
Handheld uses [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] with no [[anti-aliasing|Anti-aliasing (AA)]], so the image can look jagged on the small screen.

reviews.headline: 1080p docked / 720p handheld · 30fps
reviews.overview: DF called Luigi's Mansion 3 a shocking technical feat for Switch, with rich lighting, physics and materials. Years later, in 2024, DF named it the most technically impressive game on the console.

findings.text: Luigi's flashlight lights the rooms in real time and casts moving shadows, and the hotel's surfaces react to light convincingly, closer to a [[physically based|Physically based rendering (PBR)]] look than most Switch games.
Furniture, curtains and objects react to Luigi's vacuum with detailed [[physics|Physics / destruction]], which makes each room feel interactive.
Handheld mode trims some effects to keep 30 frames per second, so it looks a little blurrier than docked, but the overall look holds up well.

reviews.game: The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening
reviews.headline: 720p handheld · jumps between 60 and 30
reviews.overview: DF found Link's Awakening a fantastic game held back by frame-rate hiccups, especially in the overworld. Their testing pointed to the graphics chip, not the processor, as the bottleneck. The Switch 2 free update later fixed it.

findings.text: The game moves between 60 and 30 frames per second, with most problems in the overworld, including a drop just after leaving the first hut. Each [[stutter|Stutter / hitch]] is brief, and the game returns to 60 within a couple of seconds.

DF ran a clever test by overclocking the Switch. Raising the processor speed by 75% made no difference, while raising the graphics clock helped, and running at handheld resolution with docked clocks fixed nearly every hiccup. So the game is [[GPU-limited|GPU-bound / GPU-limited]], not slowed by loading data in the background as first suspected.

reviews.headline: Docked fine / handheld as low as 368p
reviews.overview: DF's main finding was that the original handheld mode had the worst image quality they had seen in a Switch game at that point, so they recommended playing docked.

findings.text: Handheld relies on heavy [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]], usually around 432p to 552p and sometimes as low as 368p, far below the 720p screen.
Strong [[sharpening|Sharpening]] tries to hide the blur, but it creates bright halos around edges, called ringing, that make the image look harsh.
DF advised playing docked. This gap was later fixed by the Switch 2 Edition, which is covered separately in the Switch 2 tab.

reviews.headline: 720–900p docked · near-locked 60fps
reviews.overview: DF's full analysis found Super Mario Odyssey pushing the Switch to its limits while keeping an almost rock-solid 60 frames per second, by letting resolution flex instead.

findings.text: Docked, [[dynamic resolution|Dynamic resolution scaling (DRS)]] moves between 720p and 900p. In handheld, the game renders moving scenes at 640×720, half the horizontal resolution, and stationary scenes at the full 1280×720, a clever trick that saves performance when the eye is least likely to notice.
Prioritizing frame rate over resolution pays off: the game holds a near rock-solid 60fps throughout.

reviews.game: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild
reviews.headline: 900p docked / 720p handheld · 30fps
reviews.overview: At launch, DF found Breath of the Wild a technical achievement in both modes, but surprisingly the handheld version ran more smoothly than docked, so they recommended playing handheld for the fewest drops.

findings.text: Docked usually holds 30 frames per second but sometimes drops briefly to 20, a pattern that suggests [[double-buffered|Double / triple buffering]] [[v-sync|V-sync]], where a missed frame falls straight to the next step down. The [[stutter|Stutter / hitch]] happens often in the open world, even in quiet scenes, and handheld mode largely avoids it.

Docked mode renders about 56% more pixels but gets only about 20% more [[memory bandwidth|Memory bandwidth]], which the processor and graphics chip share. DF's theory is that this squeeze, not raw graphics power, causes the docked stutter.

The two modes look almost identical. Docked has better [[texture filtering|Texture filtering]], adding a band of extra ground detail just ahead of Link, which most players wouldn't notice on the small handheld screen.
